Thus the dependence on a requested total-variation tolerance η\etaη is polynomial in log⁡(1/η)\log(1/\eta)log(1/η). Every output is feasible.

It also claims an exactly uniform sampler that terminates almost surely and has expected bit time polynomial in m,n,log⁡(N+1)m,n,\log(N+1)m,n,log(N+1). No fixed-dimension, balance, density, or positivity hypothesis is imposed. This exact statement has no input cell bounds or forbidden positions.

M2 claims an FPRAS for cell-bounded tables with arbitrary binary margins and bounds, including structural zeros. It detects an empty feasible set exactly and bounds bit operations on every execution, even when the estimate is inaccurate.

Its consequences include relative counting for integer arc-value vectors in explicitly given directed flow networks with finite integer capacities and prescribed vertex balances. It also gives feasible almost-uniform sampling with polynomial dependence on the inverse total-variation tolerance.

The stronger accuracy dependence and exactness of M1 should not be transferred to M2’s capped-table or flow sampler: their stated guarantees differ.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 3/5, provisional. The family would remove broad restrictions from fundamental constrained-counting problems and carefully account for the binary sizes of numerical inputs.

Uniform fixed-margin sampling can support conditional statistical comparisons: one studies how unusual an observed statistic is among tables sharing the same margins. The theorem supplies a mathematical sampling capability; whether the uniform-table model is appropriate for a particular data analysis remains an application-specific choice.

Cell bounds broaden the combinatorial reach to capacities and forbidden combinations. Their connection to integer flows makes the counting result relevant beyond literal row-and-column tables.

The exact sampler is also conceptually interesting because it separates distributional exactness from bounded execution time. Its value is not that every sample is quickly obtained under all circumstances, but that its exact law comes with a polynomial expected bit cost.

6. The main idea

Separate small coordinates from large completions

M1 treats cells incident to small margins explicitly. The remaining cells form a complete rectangle with large margins. Padding that rectangle ensures that each conditional completion problem has a dense structure suitable for geometric sampling methods.

An explicit small cell has two temporary values, representing its row and column contributions. In a balanced state they agree. Auxiliary states allow a positive discrepancy in one cell and a negative discrepancy in another, providing paths through the state space.

The weight of a small-cell state is the number of large-rectangle completions. Sampling according to these weights and then uniformly completing gives equal mass to complete state-and-completion pairs. An acceptance step removes the padding and recovers an original table.

The implemented sampler does not enumerate all completions. The manuscript instead approximates the required draws using scaled grids and rational computations, then controls the accumulated distributional error.

Correct a very accurate law exactly

A sufficiently accurate finite sampler can be mixed with a small correction distribution so that the resulting law is exactly uniform. Most runs use the fast approximate procedure; a very rare branch performs exhaustive work to draw from the remaining probability mass.

Small total-variation error alone is not a license to assert efficient exact correction. M1 establishes additional control of its actual implemented finite output law, including fallbacks and stopping rules. The correction probability is chosen small enough that the expensive branch still contributes only polynomial expected cost.

This is the precise reason the exact theorem has expected, rather than every-execution, polynomial time.

Handle arbitrary cell capacities without expanding them

M2 first tightens every cell to its attainable interval using flow feasibility. In the graph of large cells, a spanning forest lets some entries be determined from the margins once the remaining free entries are specified.

Only cells with polynomially bounded ranges are expanded into labeled binary choices. Since several labeled choices can describe the same table, reciprocal binomial and factorial corrections cancel this multiplicity on the target states.

Large free ranges are treated through weighted completion sums with soft penalties for constraint violations. Annealing strengthens those penalties. A chain with balanced defect types estimates ratios of successive weighted counts, whose product yields the desired approximation.

The paper uses two related weight extensions for different algebraic inequalities. They agree on target states but serve complementary roles in controlling movement and defect masses. This avoids assuming that one convenient weighting automatically supplies every property needed for counting.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

Exact uniform sampling is asserted here for ordinary uncapped tables. Arbitrary forbidden cells belong to the separate counting and approximate-sampling result.

The algorithms are asymptotic constructions with deliberately large polynomial exponents. Neither manuscript presents a practical performance benchmark or proves that a familiar local table-switching implementation already satisfies all these guarantees.

The target objects are integer tables or integer flow vectors, each counted once. Distinguishable-object assignments, weighted statistical models, and sampling only polytope vertices are different distributions.

Sharper running times, simpler samplers, and exact sampling with the full capped-table generality are natural further questions beyond the stated family guarantees.

8. Sources and further reading

M1’s first theorem is the key reference for exactness, accuracy-bit dependence, and expected time. M2’s first theorem gives the capped-table count and every-execution bit bound. Their introductions explicitly compare the dimension, capacity, and computational-model assumptions of earlier work.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, Exact Uniform Sampling of Contingency Tables with Arbitrary Margins (September 24, 2026).
  • M2. OpenAI, An FPRAS for Cell-Bounded Contingency Tables (September 24, 2026).

Sources consulted on 9 October 2026 at repository revision fd4aeeb. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: Uniform identity testing for noncommutative formulas
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 116 · Theoretical computer science
Importance 4/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-09

Two algebraic expressions may look different while computing exactly the same object. Identity testing asks whether their difference is identically zero. When multiplication is noncommutative, matrix substitutions preserve information that scalar substitutions erase. Family 116 claims small deterministic collections of such substitutions that work universally for every formula up to a given size.

1. The question

For ordinary numbers, xy−yx=0xy-yx=0xy−yx=0. For matrices, multiplication order matters, and XY−YXXY-YXXY−YX can be nonzero. An identity test that substitutes only numbers would therefore miss a genuinely nonzero noncommutative expression.

Random matrix substitutions can often detect nonzero expressions. The harder goal is to construct a guaranteed test deterministically, using only a bound on formula size and the number of variables, before seeing any coefficients.

The family claims one polynomial-dimensional matrix tuple for division-free formulas in characteristic zero, another construction in every positive characteristic, and polynomial-size hitting lists for rational formulas over Q\mathbb QQ. Rational formulas allow inverses, so the test must also respect where the original expression is defined.

2. Background and essential definitions

Words replace ordinary monomials

In a noncommutative polynomial, x1x2x_1x_2x1​x2​ and x2x1x_2x_1x2​x1​ are different words. Multiplication concatenates words in order. A polynomial is a finite linear combination of these words, with scalar coefficients from a field.

A division-free formula is a rooted tree with variable or scalar leaves and binary addition or ordered multiplication gates. Tree structure matters: shared subexpressions in a general circuit can encode more work than a formula of the same stated size.

Size counts every vertex, including leaves. A small formula can still expand into exponentially many words. The ordered product of many copies of x1+x2x_1+x_2x1​+x2​, for example, makes an independent choice of letter at every position.

Hitting points and black-box access

A tuple T=(T1,…,Tn)T=(T_1,\ldots,T_n)T=(T1​,…,Tn​) of square matrices is a hitting point for a class if every nonzero polynomial fff in the class satisfies

f(T1,…,Tn)≠0.f(T_1,\ldots,T_n)\ne0.f(T1​,…,Tn​)=0.

A hitting list permits several tuples and requires at least one successful evaluation. Scalars in the formula are interpreted as scalar multiples of the identity matrix.

A white-box algorithm can examine the formula’s internal gates. A black-box algorithm receives evaluations without inspecting that structure. A universal hitting construction is especially strong: it chooses its tests independently of the particular formula or its coefficients.

Characteristic and rational expressions

The characteristic of a field is zero if repeated addition of one never gives zero, and is a prime ppp otherwise. The rational numbers have characteristic zero; arithmetic modulo a prime has characteristic ppp.

A rational formula also has inverse gates. A matrix evaluation is defined only when every inverted intermediate matrix is invertible. Algebraic cancellation does not remove these domain requirements: x−1−x−1x^{-1}-x^{-1}x−1−x−1 is zero wherever defined, but its original expression is still undefined at a singular matrix.

The rational manuscript calls a formula admissible if it has at least one defined evaluation on rational matrices of some positive dimension. It is nonzero if some defined rational evaluation is nonzero.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Nisan’s 1991 work connected noncommutative computational complexity with ranks of coefficient matrices. Ordered words admit linear-algebraic representations that do not behave like ordinary commutative monomials.

Raz and Shpilka gave deterministic polynomial-time identity testing for noncommutative formulas and algebraic branching programs when their descriptions are available. Thus the new family is not the first deterministic test for this model; the challenge is universal black-box evaluation.

Bogdanov and Wee developed randomized matrix-evaluation tests. Forbes and Shpilka constructed deterministic quasipolynomial-size hitting sets for noncommutative branching programs under a field-size condition. Quasipolynomial means a running time like an exponential of a fixed power of the logarithm, generally larger than polynomial.

For rational formulas, Hrubeš and Wigderson developed reductions to linear-matrix singularity. Operator scaling and constructive noncommutative-rank algorithms subsequently supplied deterministic polynomial-time methods using the given coefficients.

Arvind, Chatterjee, and Mukhopadhyay obtained deterministic quasipolynomial hitting sets for rational formulas with unrestricted inverse nesting. They already account for matrix evaluation domains; unrestricted nesting is not itself the new feature here.

The manuscripts claim polynomial bounds for coefficient-independent test generation. They also distinguish formula size from sparsity: a test efficient in the number of expanded words need not be efficient in the size of a compact formula.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

M2 treats characteristic zero. Given positive integers n,sn,sn,s, it constructs rational matrices in deterministic polynomial bit time, with dimension

d≤2ns2,d\le2ns^2,d≤2ns2,

such that one tuple detects every nonzero division-free formula of size at most sss in nnn variables. The same tuple works over every characteristic-zero coefficient field, with rational entries interpreted through the natural embedding.

M1 treats positive characteristic. Given a promised prime ppp in binary and n,sn,sn,s in unary, one machine outputs a tuple over Fp\mathbb F_pFp​ of dimension

d=O(n3s6)d=O(n^3s^6)d=O(n3s6)

in bit time polynomial in n+s+log⁡pn+s+\log pn+s+logp. It works over every extension field of that characteristic, including characteristic two and with no assumption that ppp exceeds the formula size.

Both papers also treat their stated acyclic algebraic path-program models, where one sums ordered products along directed paths. Their precise edge-label and size conventions remain relevant; the family does not extend these claims to arbitrary shared circuits.

M3 treats rational formulas over Q\mathbb QQ. It constructs a polynomial-size list of rational matrix tuples, with polynomial dimensions, entry lengths, and total output length. Every nonzero admissible size-sss formula has a defined evaluation with invertible value at some tuple.

That last conclusion is stronger than merely obtaining a nonzero matrix. No separate bound on inverse depth or rational constant height is imposed on the formulas detected. The polynomial bit bound concerns generating the list, not evaluating an unknown expression containing arbitrarily long constants.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 4/5, provisional. Deterministic identity testing is a central derandomization problem in algebraic complexity. Universal black-box tests replace random trial substitutions with a fixed, efficiently generated collection guaranteed to expose every nonzero formula in the stated class.

The field coverage is substantive. A characteristic-zero construction based on dividing by integers may collapse modulo a small prime. M1 claims a separate construction that works uniformly without excluding such primes.

For rational expressions, preserving all inverse-domain conditions makes the test useful for the actual expression rather than only an abstractly equivalent rational function. The bounded-size list must supply a point where the full computation is defined.

The rating reflects the methodological breadth across these formula models. It is not a claim that every form of polynomial identity testing, especially general commutative circuit testing, has thereby been derandomized.

6. The main idea

Encode many words in one power series

M2 associates each ordered word with an iterated integral, interpreted as a formal power series. Formal means that coefficients are manipulated algebraically; convergence of a numerical integral is not needed for the final matrix construction.

The encoding is faithful: distinct words are linearly independent in the required sense. A nonzero polynomial therefore becomes a nonzero series. The challenge is that its first nonzero coefficient might, in principle, occur very late.

A size-sss formula has a small acyclic path representation. This converts the associated series into an entry of a finite differential system. A bound on the order of vanishing limits how many initial coefficients can be zero.

Truncating after polynomially many coefficients therefore preserves nonvanishing. The integration operators on this finite coefficient space are rational matrices, producing the universal tuple without knowing the formula.

Replace differentiation in small characteristic

Ordinary differentiation annihilates zpz^pzp in characteristic ppp, and formal integration would require divisions that may be invalid. M1 instead uses a multiplicative shift

σ(g)(z)=g(tz),\sigma(g)(z)=g(tz),σ(g)(z)=g(tz),

where ttt is an indeterminate. On the coefficient of zrz^rzr, the difference σ−1\sigma-1σ−1 acts by multiplication by tr−1t^r-1tr−1, which remains nonzero in every characteristic.

The paper establishes a corresponding vanishing-order bound, truncates the series, and then removes the indeterminate by representing multiplication in a finite truncated algebra with matrices over the prime field. This preserves bounded-degree information without assuming a conveniently large finite extension.

Certify every inverse simultaneously

M3 translates a rational formula into a bounded collection of affine matrix pencils—matrices whose entries are affine-linear expressions in the variables. Their simultaneous invertibility certifies both the domain conditions and invertibility of the final value.

The construction first uses subspace expansion to make ranks nearly full. A division-algebra lift forces the remaining ranks into multiples of a block size, turning a sufficiently small rank deficit into full rank.

Finally, bounded-degree determinant conditions are specialized on a fixed small integer grid. At least one grid point preserves all required nonvanishing conditions. Rational matrix representations remove auxiliary algebraic constants, giving the explicit list.

Formula-specific witnesses are used in the argument that the list works. The generator does not search for or receive those witnesses.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The polynomial resource guarantees refer to test construction and output size. Evaluation over an unspecified coefficient field is an exact operation with its own representation costs. Arbitrarily large rational constants cannot be processed for free simply because the list is small.

The division-free guarantees cover their stated characteristics, whereas the rational-formula list is asserted over Q\mathbb QQ. It should not be transferred to finite fields without a corresponding theorem.

Admissibility is part of M3’s promise. Undefined evaluations must be reported as such, rather than interpreted as zero. Testing arbitrary shared circuits or removing model restrictions remains outside the family claims.

8. Sources and further reading

M2 gives the characteristic-zero power-series construction; M1 explains the shift replacement required in positive characteristic. M3 states the rational-expression domain conventions and the separate cost of evaluating coefficients. Their introductions provide the white-box versus black-box comparisons needed to interpret the advance.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, Uniform Matrix Hitting Points in Every Positive Characteristic (October 4, 2026).
  • M2. OpenAI, One Rational Matrix Hitting Point for Noncommutative Formulas (September 24, 2026).
  • M3. OpenAI, Polynomial Hitting Lists for Noncommutative Rational Formulas (September 24, 2026).

Sources consulted on 9 October 2026 at repository revision fd4aeeb. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: Approximate counting of common integer polymatroid bases
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 114 · Theoretical computer science
Importance 3/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-09

Many allocation problems impose two overlapping systems of capacity constraints. Finding one feasible allocation can be tractable while counting all feasible allocations is much harder. Family 114 claims randomized relative counting for common bases of two arbitrary matroids, then extends this to integer polymatroids with potentially enormous binary-encoded capacities.

1. The question

Suppose resources must be allocated among several coordinates. One system limits combinations of coordinates in one way, while a second system imposes different limits. The task is to count allocations satisfying both systems and using the required total amount.

Even when each system separately has a well-behaved exchange structure, their intersection need not retain it. Moving one unit or swapping one selected element can violate one of the two sets of constraints.

A second challenge is numerical size. A capacity of a billion needs only about thirty binary digits. An algorithm that creates one object per capacity unit is not polynomial in the encoded input length.

The manuscripts address both issues. M2 treats ordinary matroid bases; M1 treats integer allocations and explicitly counts each vector once, without weighting it by the number of ways to assign labels to its units.

2. Background and essential definitions

Matroids and common bases

A matroid is a finite set EEE together with independent subsets. Independence is preserved by taking subsets, and any smaller independent set can be enlarged using an element of a larger one. Linear independence of vectors and cycle-free sets of graph edges are standard examples.

The rank r(A)r(A)r(A) is the maximum size of an independent subset of AAA. A basis is a maximal independent subset of the full ground set; all bases have the same size.

For two matroids on the same ground set and of equal rank, a common basis is a set that is a basis in both. If the ground set is the edges of a bipartite graph, one matroid can allow at most one selected edge at each left vertex and the other at most one at each right vertex. Their common full-size bases are perfect matchings.

Polymatroids permit integer amounts

A polymatroid replaces zero–one selection by nonnegative quantities. Its capacity function rrr assigns a nonnegative integer to every subset of EEE. It is normalized, meaning r(∅)=0r(\varnothing)=0r(∅)=0, nondecreasing, and submodular:

r(A)+r(B)≥r(A∪B)+r(A∩B).r(A)+r(B)\ge r(A\cup B)+r(A\cap B).r(A)+r(B)≥r(A∪B)+r(A∩B).

Submodularity expresses a diminishing-returns structure. The extra capacity associated with adding coordinates becomes smaller when more coordinates are already present.

For x=(xj)j∈Ex=(x_j)_{j\in E}x=(xj​)j∈E​, write x(A)=∑j∈Axjx(A)=\sum_{j\in A}x_jx(A)=∑j∈A​xj​. Given two such functions r1,r2r_1,r_2r1​,r2​ with equal total rank RRR, the family of common integer bases is

Ω={x∈Z≥0E:x(E)=R, x(A)≤ri(A) for all A⊆E, i=1,2}.\Omega=\{x\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}^{E}:x(E)=R,\ x(A)\le r_i(A)\text{ for all }A\subseteq E,\ i=1,2\}.Ω={x∈Z≥0E​:x(E)=R, x(A)≤ri​(A) for all A⊆E, i=1,2}.

Every distinct integer vector counts once. If the only constraint is allocating two units between two coordinates, the vectors (2,0),(1,1),(0,2)(2,0),(1,1),(0,2)(2,0),(1,1),(0,2) are three objects. Giving the units distinct labels would represent the middle vector twice, changing the counting measure.

Oracle access and approximation

An exact rank-value oracle returns ri(A)r_i(A)ri​(A) when queried with a subset AAA. It avoids explicitly listing exponentially many inequalities. Oracle calls are counted separately from the algorithm’s other bit operations; the internal work of the oracle is not included.

An FPRAS, or fully polynomial randomized approximation scheme, estimates Z=∣Ω∣Z=|\Omega|Z=∣Ω∣ within relative error ε\varepsilonε with failure probability at most δ\deltaδ, using polynomial resources in input length, ε−1\varepsilon^{-1}ε−1, and log⁡(1/δ)\log(1/\delta)log(1/δ).

3. Development history and previous partial results

Edmonds’s matroid intersection theory established a fundamental distinction: finding and optimizing common independent sets can be efficient through independence queries. Counting all solutions requires additional ideas.

For one matroid, Feder and Mihail obtained sampling and counting results for balanced matroids, using negative dependence. Later work treated strongly Rayleigh distributions, another structured class with strong algebraic properties.

Anari, Liu, Oveis Gharan, and Vinzant removed these special assumptions for counting bases of a single arbitrary matroid. Their high-dimensional walks use log-concave polynomials to control random movement among bases.

Intersections remained harder. Anari, Oveis Gharan, and Vinzant obtained an exponential-in-rank factor approximation in polynomial time and relative approximation with exponential-in-rank running time. The latter becomes fully polynomial for small logarithmic rank, but not for arbitrary rank.

The permanent FPRAS of Jerrum, Sinclair, and Vigoda already solves a special common-basis case arising from two partition matroids. Its strategy of balancing nearly feasible states is an important methodological predecessor.

For integer allocations, Brändén and Huh’s Lorentzian polynomial theory provides powerful concavity properties. However, a factorial-normalized generating polynomial weights integer vectors differently from a uniform count. Nor does good behavior for one polymatroid automatically transfer to the intersection of two.

M1 builds on M2 and on the cell-bounded contingency-table construction in family 115. Its added task is to handle arbitrary submodular rank constraints and large binary capacities while preserving the intended one-vector-one-vote count.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

M2 claims an FPRAS for common bases of two equal-rank matroids given only exact independence oracles. No matrix representation, graph representation, or generating-polynomial evaluation oracle is required.

It also derives counting schemes for common independent sets of prescribed, unrestricted, or maximum cardinality, including when the two matroid ranks differ. Its almost-uniform samplers always return feasible objects on nonempty instances and detect emptiness exactly.

M1 claims an FPRAS for the common integer bases defined above, with RRR supplied in binary and exact rank-value oracles. It returns a nonnegative rational estimate satisfying

Pr⁡[(1−ε)Z≤Z^≤(1+ε)Z]≥1−δ.\Pr[(1-\varepsilon)Z\le\widehat Z\le(1+\varepsilon)Z]\ge1-\delta.Pr[(1−ε)Z≤Z≤(1+ε)Z]≥1−δ.

On every execution, the number of oracle calls and the bit work outside the oracles are bounded by a fixed polynomial in ground-set size, binary input length, ε−1\varepsilon^{-1}ε−1, and log⁡(1/δ)\log(1/\delta)log(1/δ).

An empty feasible set always produces zero. If R=0R=0R=0, the unique common base is the zero vector. Lower-dimensional feasible regions are included; the theorem does not require an interior in the ambient coordinate space.

The polynomials have large fixed exponents. The claimed contribution is polynomial dependence on the correct input encoding, rather than an optimized implementation.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 3/5, provisional. The family would provide a general counting framework for intersecting combinatorial capacity systems, substantially extending the cases addressed by single-matroid methods.

Its oracle formulation is broad: a rank function can describe a feasible system without revealing an explicit matrix or an exponentially long list of inequalities. The result makes clear which information the counting algorithm actually needs.

Binary capacities are equally substantive. A theorem polynomial in the numerical capacity can be exponential in the length of the input. M1 claims to avoid that blowup while also avoiding the counting bias introduced by labeled expansions.

These are structural and asymptotic guarantees. The score reflects a substantial advance within counting and discrete optimization, while recognizing its specialized input model and the lack of a practical runtime claim.

6. The main idea

Turn two matroids into a paired selection problem

M2 makes two copies of the ground set, pairing corresponding elements. It combines the first matroid with the dual of the second. A dual matroid has as bases the complements of the original bases.

Selecting exactly one element from every pair is called a transversal. With the combined matroid chosen as in the paper, a transversal is a basis exactly when it represents a common basis of the original two systems.

The algorithm gives a positive but small weight to rank-deficient transversals. It also permits temporary defects: one empty pair and one doubly selected pair. These extra states provide routes between feasible selections that might otherwise be far apart.

Learn how to balance defects

Different defect types can have very different total weights. Multipliers are learned during an annealing schedule to keep them from overwhelming the target transversals or becoming too rare to be useful.

Algebraic inequalities control transport between conditional distributions and variation in the observables the algorithm estimates. The manuscript deliberately distinguishes this from proving fast mixing for every fluctuation inside every defect class.

A trace chain records successive returns to transversals. Controlling that chain and the relevant frequency estimates is sufficient for the counting procedure. The analytical partition sums and flows are not extra oracles supplied to the implementation.

Keep large ranges implicit

M1 cannot expand a huge capacity into that many pairs. Instead it finds a rational center of the common-base region and identifies near-tight constraints. These define partitions whose part totals have only polynomially many relevant discrete values.

Large remaining ranges are treated through weighted integration over free coordinates. Soft penalties suppress violations of the original constraints. Convex-volume approximation supplies numerical estimates of the resulting weights.

Integration preserves an ordinary form of log concavity, but the discrete counting framework needs stronger quadratic inequalities. The manuscript smooths and adjusts the weights, controls the difference between discrete changes and continuous derivatives, and establishes the needed inequalities for its particular construction.

Only bounded-range variables are expanded into paired labels. Factorial corrections cancel the multiplicities on target transversals, restoring unit mass per original integer vector.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The rank functions are promised to satisfy the polymatroid axioms and to be available through exact value queries. The theorem does not provide an efficient test that an arbitrary black box satisfies those promises, nor does it include the black box’s internal computational cost.

The main integer-base theorem assumes equal total ranks. M2’s unequal-rank consequences concern common independent sets and should not be substituted indiscriminately for that hypothesis.

Counting each integer vector once is part of the problem definition. Applications requiring distinguishable units, factorial weights, or a different probability law need their own translation.

The result leaves practical efficiency, sharper polynomial exponents, and extensions to broader non-submodular constraints as separate questions. Its methods exploit the particular exchange and concavity structure of matroids and polymatroids.

8. Sources and further reading

M2 gives the paired-matroid reduction and its independence-oracle guarantees. M1 states the binary-capacity theorem and identifies the exact companion inputs it uses. The primary historical papers linked above explain why optimization, single-system counting, and intersection counting require different levels of machinery.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, An FPRAS for Common Integer Polymatroid Bases with Binary Capacities (October 5, 2026).
  • M2. OpenAI, Approximate counting of common bases of two matroids (September 23, 2026).

Sources consulted on 9 October 2026 at repository revision fd4aeeb. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: Uniform sparsest cut hardness and semidefinite gaps
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 117 · Theoretical computer science
Importance 4/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-09

A network can be difficult to divide even when a geometric relaxation suggests a cheap separation. Family 117 studies two distinct obstacles: the computational hardness of finding a near-optimal uniform sparsest cut, and the quantitative error of a standard semidefinite relaxation. Both claims preserve equal demand between every pair of vertices, a restriction that substantially changes the problem.

1. The question

A cut divides the vertices of a graph into two nonempty parts. Crossing edges represent connections disrupted by that division. Minimizing crossing capacity alone can isolate one inexpensive vertex, even when that is not a useful global separation.

Uniform sparsest cut divides the crossing capacity by the number of vertex pairs separated. For nnn vertices and one side SSS, that number is ∣S∣(n−∣S∣)|S|(n-|S|)∣S∣(n−∣S∣).

The question is how cheaply the network can be divided relative to this all-pairs demand. Can a polynomial-time algorithm always return a cut within a fixed constant factor of the best one? And how closely does the standard vector relaxation track the true optimum?

The manuscripts claim a negative answer to constant-factor approximation under P≠NP\mathsf P e\mathsf{NP}P=NP, and a nearly square-root-logarithmic separation between the relaxation and the actual cut value.

2. Background and essential definitions

Capacities, demands, and the objective

Let cij=cji≥0c_{ij}=c_{ji}\ge0cij​=cji​≥0 be the capacity between distinct vertices i,ji,ji,j. Missing edges can be assigned capacity zero. The objective is

Φ(G)=min⁡∅≠S⊊V∑i∈S, j∉Scij∣S∣(n−∣S∣).\Phi(G)=\min_{\varnothing e S\subsetneq V} rac{\sum_{i\in S,\,j otin S}c_{ij}}{|S|(n-|S|)}.Φ(G)=∅=S⊊Vmin​∣S∣(n−∣S∣)∑i∈S,j∈/S​cij​​.

Each crossing unordered pair is counted once in the numerator. The denominator gives unit demand to every distinct pair, regardless of whether it is an edge.

A factor-CCC approximation must return an actual nonempty proper cut with value at most CΦ(G)C\Phi(G)CΦ(G). The factor is multiplicative. A fixed additive error can be useless when the optimum is very small.

The nonuniform problem replaces the denominator by selected or weighted demands. Hardness or geometric obstructions for that broader problem do not automatically establish the uniform case.

Relax cuts into vector distances

A cut has a simple distance representation: assign zero to vertices on one side and one to those on the other. Distances are zero within a side and one across it.

The Goemans–Linial semidefinite relaxation permits more general distances

d(i,j)=∥vi−vj∥22,d(i,j)=\|v_i-v_j\|_2^2,d(i,j)=∥vi​−vj​∥22​,

subject to every triangle inequality. Squared Euclidean distances do not automatically satisfy those inequalities, so that condition is essential. Distinct vertices may have distance zero, giving a semimetric.

After normalizing ∑i<jd(i,j)=1\sum_{i<j}d(i,j)=1∑i<j​d(i,j)=1, the relaxation minimizes ∑i<jcijd(i,j)\sum_{i<j}c_{ij}d(i,j)∑i<j​cij​d(i,j). Write its value as GL⁡(G)\operatorname{GL}(G)GL(G). Every normalized cut distance is feasible, hence

GL⁡(G)≤Φ(G).\operatorname{GL}(G)\le\Phi(G).GL(G)≤Φ(G).

The integrality gap is the ratio Φ(G)/GL⁡(G)\Phi(G)/\operatorname{GL}(G)Φ(G)/GL(G) when the denominator is positive. A large gap says the relaxation can be too optimistic, even if solved exactly.

3. Development history and previous partial results

The flow–cut approach of Leighton and Rao linked graph partitioning to routing many simultaneous demands and gave logarithmic approximation guarantees. Linial, London, and Rabinovich developed the metric-embedding viewpoint connecting cuts with geometry.

Arora, Rao, and Vazirani, first presented in 2004, improved uniform sparsest-cut approximation to order log⁡n\sqrt{\log n}logn​ through semidefinite programming and geometric separation. That is the upper-bound benchmark for this family.

Exact NP-hardness does not by itself rule out a constant-factor approximation. Earlier strong approximation hardness for uniform sparsest cut used additional assumptions such as Small-Set Expansion, as reviewed in M1. Related Unique Games implications for nonuniform demands concern a different objective.

On the relaxation side, Devanur, Khot, Saket, and Vishnoi established a growing uniform-demand integrality gap of order log⁡log⁡n\log\log nloglogn, disproving the constant-gap prediction. Kane and Meka obtained a stronger lower bound of the form exp⁡(Ω(log⁡log⁡n))\exp(\Omega(\sqrt{\log\log n}))exp(Ω(loglogn​)).

For general demands, geometric work culminated in a square-root-logarithmic lower bound by Naor and Young, with matching upper bounds in later work of Chang, Naor, and Ren. But worst-pair distortion is not the same as preservation of average distances over every pair.

Rabinovich’s average-distortion framework identifies the relevant geometric quantity for uniform demands. The new gap manuscript addresses precisely that average-distance obstruction, rather than simply importing a general-demand example.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

M1 states that for every fixed C>1C>1C>1, a deterministic polynomial-time reduction maps a Boolean satisfiability instance to a rational-capacity graph and positive rational threshold aaa such that

satisfiable  ⟹  Φ(G)≤a,unsatisfiable  ⟹  Φ(G)>Ca. egin{aligned} ext{satisfiable}&\implies\Phi(G)\le a,\ ext{unsatisfiable}&\implies\Phi(G)>Ca.\end{aligned}satisfiableunsatisfiable​⟹Φ(G)≤a,⟹Φ(G)>Ca.​

Every distinct vertex pair has demand exactly one. Graph size and number encodings are polynomial in the source input, with constants and polynomial degree allowed to depend on CCC.

Thus every fixed-factor approximation is NP-hard. The reduction itself uses no unproved complexity assumption; concluding that no polynomial-time approximation exists additionally assumes P≠NP\mathsf P e\mathsf{NP}P=NP. The direct uniform-demand reduction is independent of the family’s cited nonuniform consequence of Unique Games.

M2 claims a sequence of instances on nj→∞n_j o\inftynj​→∞ vertices with positive relaxation value and

Φ(Gj)GL⁡(Gj)≥clog⁡nj(log⁡log⁡nj)3 rac{\Phi(G_j)}{\operatorname{GL}(G_j)}\ge c rac{\sqrt{\log n_j}}{(\log\log n_j)^3}GL(Gj​)Φ(Gj​)​≥c(loglognj​)3lognj​​​

for an absolute c>0c>0c>0. Its capacities are nonnegative real numbers and its demands are exactly uniform. The construction is stated along an infinite sequence of sizes, not as an instance for every integer size.

This approaches the square-root-logarithmic upper-bound scale up to an iterated-logarithmic factor. It concerns the basic Goemans–Linial relaxation, not every possible strengthened hierarchy.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 4/5, provisional. Sparsest cut is a central graph-partitioning problem with connections to flows, approximation algorithms, and metric geometry. The claims would strengthen both its computational hardness landscape and the quantitative understanding of its main geometric relaxation.

The two results answer different questions. An integrality gap identifies a limitation of one relaxation; it does not rule out a completely different algorithm. NP-hardness constrains all polynomial-time approximation methods under the usual complexity separation, but does not specify how inaccurate one relaxation can be.

Uniform demands make the advance more specific and meaningful. Every pair contributes, so a construction cannot concentrate all demand on a carefully chosen collection of difficult pairs. It must create an obstruction visible in the global average.

6. The main idea

Make even very small cuts meaningful

M1 builds a gap reduction from local tests of a proposed Boolean assignment. A satisfying assignment induces a cheap cut. Conversely, a sufficiently cheap cut must contain information that can be decoded into a satisfying assignment.

The difficult case is a cut with a tiny side. Its separated demand can be very small, so an absolute error allowance could overwhelm the quantity being compared. The construction tracks errors relative to the cut’s own demand, expressed through the variance of its zero–one indicator.

The paper uses rare events built from conjunctions of predicates, meaning yes-or-no tests on proof bits. A low comparison cost forces a signal from which a consistent Boolean valuation can be extracted. Different descriptions of the same predicate must receive the same valuation; this keeps the decoding tied to functions rather than arbitrary encodings.

Finally, rational approximations and replication convert probability masses into vertex counts. Heavy connections prevent a cheap cut from separating copies improperly. This produces the exact cardinality-product denominator rather than an approximately uniform demand model.

Build distances that cuts cannot preserve on average

M2 takes a geometric route. Finite distances arising from cuts can be combined into distances in ℓ1\ell_1ℓ1​, where

∥z∥1=∑i∣zi∣.\|z\|_1=\sum_i|z_i|.∥z∥1​=i∑​∣zi​∣.

A map is nonexpanding if it never increases pairwise distances. The construction seeks a squared-Euclidean semimetric with large average distance, but for which every nonexpanding map into ℓ1\ell_1ℓ1​ has much smaller average distance.

It creates many rounded coordinate charts from a common parameter cube. Different charts describe the same underlying parameter values, forcing a candidate map to respect several compatible sets of local constraints.

Hilbert-space features give large global distances. A separate repair enforces all triangle inequalities while preserving carefully controlled small costs across neighboring cells. Both local and global estimates are necessary: a uniformly small absolute error could still destroy the tiny interface bounds.

The many charts then constrain gradients of smoothed versions of any ℓ1\ell_1ℓ1​ map. Those gradient bounds limit the average distances the map can retain.

Convert geometry into a graph instance

The geometric probability measure is replaced by multiplicities of vertices, retaining every chart’s constraints. Uniform measure on the copies approximates the intended average while giving equal demand to each pair.

A finite-dimensional duality between cuts and capacities then produces the claimed graph instance. The geometric dimension-to-vertex-count conversion accounts for the displayed (log⁡log⁡n)3(\log\log n)^3(loglogn)3 loss.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The hardness factor is any fixed constant. The reduction’s degree may depend on that constant, so it does not automatically yield a quantitative hardness bound growing with nnn.

The gap theorem is existential with real capacities, whereas the hardness reduction supplies rational encodings in polynomial time. These are separate output guarantees.

The gap nearly reaches the known upper-bound order but leaves iterated-logarithmic slack. Removing that slack, understanding stronger relaxations, and obtaining more quantitative approximation-hardness rates are distinct further questions.

The family also leaves room for efficient algorithms on restricted graph classes or with additional promises. Worst-case hardness does not describe every network instance.

8. Sources and further reading

M1’s theorem specifies the reduction, capacity encoding, and every-cut scope. M2 defines its semidefinite relaxation explicitly and traces the average-distortion route to uniform demands. The historical papers linked above explain why computational hardness and geometric relaxation gaps must be assessed separately.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, Constant-factor hardness of uniform sparsest cut (2026).
  • M2. OpenAI, Near-square-root logarithmic integrality gaps for uniform sparsest cut (2026).

Sources consulted on 9 October 2026 at repository revision fd4aeeb. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: Unbounded bin-packing gaps and the modified integer round-up conjecture
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 118 · Theoretical computer science
Importance 3/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-09

Bin packing asks how many unit-capacity containers are needed for a collection of items. A powerful linear relaxation permits fractional numbers of feasible bin patterns, often giving a remarkably accurate lower bound. Family 118 claims that the discrepancy between this fractional value and a real packing is nevertheless unbounded, and that no fixed additive approximation allowance is efficiently attainable unless P equals NP.

1. The question

Each item has a rational size between zero and one. Items must be assigned whole to bins, with total size at most one in each bin. The objective is to minimize the number of bins.

Suppose a fractional optimization method says that one hundred bins should suffice. Must a genuine packing fit into one hundred and one? Or can an unavoidable extra cost grow beyond every fixed number of bins?

The modified integer round-up conjecture predicted a very small discrepancy: round the fractional optimum up to an integer, then allow one additional bin. The manuscript claims counterexamples with arbitrarily large additive gaps.

A related but distinct question asks whether an algorithm can always construct a packing using at most a fixed number of bins beyond the true optimum. The same paper claims hardness for every such fixed allowance.

2. Background and essential definitions

Integral packings and configurations

Write OPT⁡(I)\operatorname{OPT}(I)OPT(I) for the minimum number of bins for an instance III. A configuration is any collection of item sizes whose total is at most one: it describes one feasible bin pattern.

If SSS is the set of distinct numerical sizes and nσn_\sigmanσ​ is the number of items of size σ\sigmaσ, a type configuration is an integer vector c=(cσ)c=(c_\sigma)c=(cσ​) satisfying

∑σ∈Sσcσ≤1.\sum_{\sigma\in S}\sigma c_\sigma\le1.σ∈S∑​σcσ​≤1.

The configuration linear program chooses nonnegative real weights zcz_czc​, interpreted as fractional numbers of bins of each pattern, and minimizes

OPT⁡LP(I)=min⁡{∑czc:∑ccσzc≥nσ for every σ}.\operatorname{OPT}_{\mathrm{LP}}(I)=\min\left\{\sum_c z_c:\sum_c c_\sigma z_c\ge n_\sigma\text{ for every }\sigma\right\}.OPTLP​(I)=min{c∑​zc​:c∑​cσ​zc​≥nσ​ for every σ}.

Every real packing gives a feasible integral choice of pattern weights. Hence the fractional optimum is a lower bound on the packing optimum.

Two pattern conventions

The ordinary type formulation may repeat a size within a pattern as often as capacity allows, even beyond its available input multiplicity. An individual-copy formulation instead gives every physical item a distinct identity and permits a pattern to use each at most once.

These formulations can differ. The manuscript states its main notation for the ordinary numerical-type version and separately establishes the same gap for the stronger individual-copy version on its constructed instances.

Additive and multiplicative errors

A multiplicative guarantee uses at most (1+ε)OPT⁡(1+\varepsilon)\operatorname{OPT}(1+ε)OPT bins, perhaps with an additional term. Its excess can grow as the optimum grows. At optimum one million, even one-percent error permits ten thousand extra bins.

An additive guarantee uses at most OPT⁡+C\operatorname{OPT}+COPT+C bins, where CCC is fixed independently of input size. That is a much sharper requirement for large instances.

The modified integer round-up conjecture is the structural assertion

OPT⁡(I)≤⌈OPT⁡LP(I)⌉+1.\operatorname{OPT}(I)\le\lceil\operatorname{OPT}_{\mathrm{LP}}(I)\rceil+1.OPT(I)≤⌈OPTLP​(I)⌉+1.

It predicts existence of a near-fractional packing. It does not itself supply an efficient algorithm to find one.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Configuration methods grew out of cutting-stock optimization. Gilmore and Gomory’s 1961 formulation uses linear programming over feasible cutting patterns, with column generation to avoid listing every pattern initially.

The stronger integer round-up property, which would need no extra bin after rounding, was studied by Marcotte and disproved by explicit instances. Scheithauer and Terno investigated the modified one-extra-bin proposal, followed by further theoretical work.

On the algorithmic side, Fernandez de la Vega and Lueker obtained an asymptotic approximation scheme: for fixed accuracy, the multiplicative ratio approaches one on sufficiently large optima. That still permits an unbounded additive discrepancy.

Karmarkar and Karp combined grouping with configuration-LP methods to obtain a logarithmic-squared additive bound. Discrepancy-based rounding later improved this to order log⁡OPT⁡ log⁡log⁡OPT⁡\log\operatorname{OPT}\,\log\log\operatorname{OPT}logOPTloglogOPT, and Hoberg and Rothvoss achieved logarithmic additive loss.

Earlier discrepancy constructions showed that algorithms confined to rounding the support of a particular fractional solution could need many extra bins. But an unrestricted integral packing can use other configurations. A lower bound for one rounding method therefore does not by itself prove a gap for the full configuration LP.

This distinction motivates the new manuscript’s extraction argument: it must analyze every sufficiently small packing, including those using unintended combinations of items.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

For every integer c≥0c\ge0c≥0, M1 claims a finite rational bin-packing instance and an integer BBB such that

OPT⁡LP(I)=B,OPT⁡(I)>B+c.\operatorname{OPT}_{\mathrm{LP}}(I)=B,\qquad\operatorname{OPT}(I)>B+c.OPTLP​(I)=B,OPT(I)>B+c.

The same fractional value is obtained in the individual-copy formulation. Because BBB is already integral, the gap cannot be explained by ambiguity about taking a ceiling.

Every item is strictly larger than 1/61/61/6. Consequently each bin contains at most five items. Unbounded additive gaps therefore occur even under this fixed bound on the number of items in a bin.

Taking c=1c=1c=1 contradicts the modified integer round-up conjecture. The stronger statement is that no absolute additive upper bound holds for these configuration relaxations.

Separately, for every fixed ccc, the paper claims NP-hardness of distinguishing instances packable in BBB bins from instances not packable in B+cB+cB+c bins, again with all sizes larger than 1/61/61/6.

It follows that a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm with any fixed additive guarantee exists if and only if P=NP\mathsf P=\mathsf{NP}P=NP. The structural gap theorem itself has no complexity-class assumption; the algorithmic impossibility conclusion uses the usual separation assumption.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 3/5, provisional. The claim would settle a longstanding question about a central relaxation in packing and cutting stock, while locating a genuine barrier to constant-additive approximation.

The result changes how the fractional bound can be interpreted. It remains a valid lower bound and can remain very accurate on many instances, but it cannot support a universal promise of only one or a few additional bins.

The restriction to at most five items per bin is striking because it eliminates explanations based solely on bins containing huge numbers of tiny objects. The obstruction instead comes from how many locally feasible patterns interact globally.

The claim does not invalidate asymptotic approximation schemes or logarithmic additive upper bounds. An unbounded gap may grow slowly with instance size and remain a vanishing fraction of the total optimum.

6. The main idea

Encode a graph-cover decision in packing

The manuscript reduces from vertex cover. A vertex cover is a set of graph vertices containing at least one endpoint of every edge.

For a fixed additive allowance and a small accuracy parameter, the construction creates items with two local states for each graph vertex. Choosing the appropriate state corresponds to placing that vertex in a cover. Edge-related resources enforce that each edge has a sufficiently funded endpoint.

A small vertex cover gives an intended packing into BBB bins. Conversely, any packing into only B+cB+cB+c bins can be decoded into a vertex cover of controlled size. The converse is what makes the reduction useful for hardness.

Competing interval requirements force choices

Inside each vertex gadget, two rooted trees organize nested intervals and resource quotas. Each tree separately can satisfy a demanding path-coverage requirement. When both compete for the same quotas, they cannot simultaneously satisfy even a weaker requirement everywhere.

This forces additional global resources onto one side of the gadget. The selected side records the vertex-cover choice. Tests corresponding to graph edges are placed near the relevant intervals so that incompatible local choices cannot all be accommodated with the available resources.

The trees and intervals are analytical components of a numerical construction. The final instance is ordinary one-dimensional bin packing, with rational scalar item sizes.

Use five item roles near one fifth

An intended bin combines five roles: a row item, an anchor, two kinds of auxiliary resource, and a flag. Small perturbations of sizes near one fifth encode labels, ordering constraints, and interval endpoints.

Because all sizes exceed one sixth, no bin can contain six items. Carefully separated numerical coordinates ensure that a five-item bin fits only when the encoded conditions cooperate.

For example, an anchor can act like a deadline while auxiliary lengths determine a completion coordinate. Feasibility of that bin becomes an inequality comparing completion with deadline. Prefix counts of such inequalities translate into interval-coverage requirements.

Control unintended packings

An arbitrary packing is free to mix roles and labels. The paper assigns integer scores to items and uses conservation of total scores to show that a packing with only a fixed number of extra bins has only a bounded number of serious deviations from the intended patterns.

A second ordering argument controls mismatched labels. The error at a vertex is bounded independently of the number of internal positions in its gadget, allowing the coverage tests to retain their force.

For the structural LP gap, the paper uses a small graph and fractional mixtures of the two local states. Each local state uses its labeled items consistently, while averaging balances global inventories. A distribution over physical copies yields the fractional solution of value BBB, and the five-item bound supplies a matching lower bound on that value.

The fractional mixture can combine locally valid choices that no equally economical integral packing can realize simultaneously. This is the source of the gap.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The unbounded-gap theorem does not establish a matching logarithmic lower bound in terms of item count or optimum. The constructed instances can grow very rapidly as the prescribed gap increases.

A fixed maximum number of items per bin is different from a fixed number of distinct sizes. The construction may use many numerical sizes. Goemans and Rothvoss give polynomial-time solvability when the number of item types is fixed, a different parameter regime.

The hardness result concerns worst-case inputs and fixed additive allowances. It does not rule out useful heuristics, exact algorithms for small instances, or stronger guarantees under additional structure.

The next quantitative question is how the largest possible full-LP gap grows with instance size, beyond merely being unbounded.

8. Sources and further reading

M1’s Definitions 1.1 and Theorems 1.2–1.3 distinguish the two LP formulations, the unconditional structural gap, and the hardness reduction. The historical cutting-stock and approximation papers linked above explain why none of these statements is equivalent to the existence of a good multiplicative approximation scheme.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, Additive hardness and unbounded configuration gaps in bin packing (September 24, 2026).

Sources consulted on 9 October 2026 at repository revision fd4aeeb. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: The Courtade–Kumar and Hellinger conjectures
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 119 · Theoretical computer science
Importance 4/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-09

If you compress a collection of independent fair bits into one bit, which summary remains most informative after the original bits are independently corrupted? Family 119 claims sharp inequalities saying that a single coordinate is optimal. Its two manuscripts also distinguish a general randomized-summary theorem from a stronger-looking square-root comparison involving Hellinger affinity.

1. The question

Let X=(X1,…,Xn)X=(X_1,\ldots,X_n)X=(X1​,…,Xn​) be independent uniform signs, each equal to plus or minus one. Before noise is applied, choose a Boolean summary f(X)f(X)f(X), also taking values plus or minus one.

Each coordinate then passes through an independent bit-flip channel, producing a noisy vector YYY. A receiver sees all of YYY, rather than only one further Boolean summary. How much information about f(X)f(X)f(X) remains?

A natural candidate is a coordinate, f(X)=Xif(X)=X_if(X)=Xi​. Majority combines many inputs, while parity uses all inputs symmetrically, but combining more bits need not preserve more information about a one-bit summary.

The Courtade–Kumar conjecture says no Boolean summary beats a coordinate. The family claims this conclusion, a sharp extension to randomized binary summaries, and a separate Hellinger inequality that also implies the Boolean information bound.

2. Background and essential definitions

The noise parameter

Write Yi=XiZiY_i=X_iZ_iYi​=Xi​Zi​, where the independent noise signs satisfy EZi=ρ\mathbb E Z_i=\rhoEZi​=ρ. For ordinary flip probability ε∈[0,1/2]\varepsilon\in[0,1/2]ε∈[0,1/2],

ρ=1−2ε.\rho=1-2\varepsilon.ρ=1−2ε.

Thus ρ=1\rho=1ρ=1 means no noise and ρ=0\rho=0ρ=0 means the output is independent of the input. The manuscripts also allow negative correlation; symmetry makes absolute correlation the relevant quantity in the information bound.

Entropy and mutual information

The binary entropy in bits is

h2(p)=−plog⁡2p−(1−p)log⁡2(1−p),h_2(p)=-p\log_2p-(1-p)\log_2(1-p),h2​(p)=−plog2​p−(1−p)log2​(1−p),

with 0log⁡20=00\log_2 0=00log2​0=0. It is one for a fair bit and zero for a deterministic bit.

Mutual information I(U;Y)=H(U)−H(U∣Y)I(U;Y)=H(U)-H(U\mid Y)I(U;Y)=H(U)−H(U∣Y) measures how much observing YYY reduces uncertainty about UUU. It is not the same as the probability of predicting UUU correctly.

For a coordinate summary, the other noisy coordinates carry no extra information, and

I(Xi;Y)=1−h2(ε).I(X_i;Y)=1-h_2(\varepsilon).I(Xi​;Y)=1−h2​(ε).

The main Boolean comparison says this is an upper bound for every fff.

Randomized summaries and output bias

A randomized binary summary UUU can be described by its conditional mean

u(x)=E[U∣X=x]∈[−1,1].u(x)=\mathbb E[U\mid X=x]\in[-1,1].u(x)=E[U∣X=x]∈[−1,1].

The value u(x)u(x)u(x) determines the conditional probabilities of its two outputs. Ordinary Boolean functions are the special case u(x)∈{−1,1}u(x)\in\{-1,1\}u(x)∈{−1,1}.

The mean m=Ef(X)m=\mathbb E f(X)m=Ef(X) measures output bias. A fair input vector need not produce a fair summary: an AND-like rule may output one only rarely.

The noise operator is the conditional averaging map Tρu(y)=E[u(X)∣Y=y]T_\rho u(y)=\mathbb E[u(X)\mid Y=y]Tρ​u(y)=E[u(X)∣Y=y]. It describes the receiver’s posterior mean of the summary. A single coordinate satisfies Tρxi=ρyiT_\rho x_i=\rho y_iTρ​xi​=ρyi​.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Courtade and Kumar formulated the information question in work presented in 2013 and published in 2014. Its simple appearance hides a dimension-independent comparison over every Boolean function.

Partial results established the conjecture in high-noise regimes. Samorodnitsky proved it for all Boolean functions in a dimension-independent high-noise range. Yu’s work on stability and later local optimality enlarged ranges for balanced functions.

Other results addressed neighboring formulations. Pichler, Piantanida, and Matz proved coordinate optimality when the noisy observation is itself reduced to one Boolean output. That is not the same as letting the receiver observe the full vector.

The 2017 Hellinger conjecture of Anantharam and collaborators replaced the entropy comparison by a square-root affinity inequality and showed that it implies the Courtade–Kumar conclusion. Chen and Nair developed mean-dependent bounds and dimension-induction methods in this direction.

Chen, Gohari, and Nair proposed a differential approach: control instantaneous information loss under gradually increasing noise, then integrate the inequality. Both manuscripts in this family develop that viewpoint.

The source history also includes several September 2026 preprints announcing full Courtade–Kumar proofs, including Chen and collaborators, Ky and Tran, and Mahdavifar and Beirami. M1 explicitly acknowledges overlap: an estimate in the first of these also yields its soft-channel contraction when integrated while retaining initial information. Its additional claims concern its proof route and mean-dependent production bound. M2’s Hellinger statement is a distinct functional inequality.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

In bit units, the Boolean consequence is

I(f(X);Y)≤1−h2(ε)I(f(X);Y)\le1-h_2(\varepsilon)I(f(X);Y)≤1−h2​(ε)

for every dimension and every Boolean fff. Signed coordinates attain equality.

To state M1’s more general comparison, define

ψ(a)=1−h2 ⁣(1+a2),0≤a≤1.\psi(a)=1-h_2\!\left(\frac{1+a}{2}\right),\qquad 0\le a\le1.ψ(a)=1−h2​(21+a​),0≤a≤1.

This is increasing, so it has an inverse on [0,1][0,1][0,1]. M1 claims that every randomized binary summary satisfies

I(U;Y)≤ψ ⁣(∣ρ∣ ψ−1(I(U;X))).I(U;Y)\le\psi\!\left(|\rho|\,\psi^{-1}(I(U;X))\right).I(U;Y)≤ψ(∣ρ∣ψ−1(I(U;X))).

The papers use natural logarithms; this display is the same normalized statement in bits. A soft coordinate with u(x)=axiu(x)=a x_iu(x)=axi​ attains the bound at the corresponding initial information level.

For a deterministic summary, I(f(X);X)=H(f(X))I(f(X);X)=H(f(X))I(f(X);X)=H(f(X)). Substituting its actual output entropy gives a stricter upper curve when the output is biased. This does not assert that every fixed output bias attains that refined curve.

For M2, put K(t)=1−t2K(t)=\sqrt{1-t^2}K(t)=1−t2​. Its claim is

K(m)−EK(Tρf)≤1−K(ρ),m=Ef.K(m)-\mathbb E K(T_\rho f)\le1-K(\rho),\qquad m=\mathbb E f.K(m)−EK(Tρ​f)≤1−K(ρ),m=Ef.

It applies to every Boolean output bias and every ρ∈[−1,1]\rho\in[-1,1]ρ∈[−1,1]. Signed coordinates attain equality. M2 also reproduces the established implication from this inequality to the Boolean information bound.

M1 additionally states a mean-dependent lower bound on instantaneous entropy production, stronger than the information-only rate in specified regimes. It should be distinguished from simply restating the finite-noise Boolean conclusion.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 4/5, provisional. The problem asks for an exact extremal principle at the intersection of information theory and Boolean-function analysis. A dimension-independent sharp comparison explains how much information a single-bit compression can retain through product noise.

The randomized-summary result is especially interpretable: match two summaries by the information they initially contain, then compare how much survives. The coordinate-based summary supplies the claimed optimal curve at every initial-information level.

The Hellinger inequality connects this information question with another measure of statistical distinguishability. Its inclusion of biased outputs matters because restricting to balanced functions would omit much of the Boolean class.

The rating reflects the scope of the functional statements and methods. It does not imply exclusive priority for the ordinary Courtade–Kumar conclusion, which the manuscripts themselves compare with contemporaneous claims.

6. The main idea

Increase the noise continuously

Set ρ=e−t\rho=e^{-t}ρ=e−t, so increasing time ttt adds more noise. The operators Te−tT_{e^{-t}}Te−t​ compose like a continuous evolution.

Information decreases along this evolution. Its derivative can be expressed through local costs on edges of the discrete cube, where neighboring inputs differ in one bit. If one bounds the rate of information loss by the rate for a coordinate carrying the same information, integration yields the desired finite-noise comparison.

A linear rate estimate is not sharp enough. The coordinate curve is nonlinear, and the proof must preserve the extra information in that curvature.

Join two smaller cubes carefully

Splitting along one input coordinate produces two lower-dimensional functions. Their information-loss rates contribute, but joining them adds another cost.

M1 optimizes that joining cost while tracking both mean and conditional entropy. Its local optimizer consists of one interior pair and possibly the two corners corresponding to common deterministic outputs. The construction uses two entropy capacities and comparisons describing how adding common outputs changes the required cost.

Keeping the mean is essential: an information-only local inequality does not close the induction for every coupled pair. The manuscript combines profiles so the dimension induction survives all bias regimes.

Interpret the square-root expression

For a nonconstant Boolean summary, let P+P_+P+​ and P−P_-P−​ be the laws of the noisy vector conditional on the two summary outputs. Their Hellinger affinity is

A(P+,P−)=∑yP+(y)P−(y).A(P_+,P_-)=\sum_y\sqrt{P_+(y)P_-(y)}.A(P+​,P−​)=y∑​P+​(y)P−​(y)​.

Large affinity means the two conditional laws overlap substantially. The left side of M2’s inequality equals K(m)(1−A(P+,P−))K(m)(1-A(P_+,P_-))K(m)(1−A(P+​,P−​)), a bias-weighted distinguishability measure.

M2 combines an asymmetric dimension induction in one noise range with an energy-continuation argument in the remaining range. At a hypothetical first failure, the rate comparison would contradict the required crossing behavior. It treats different bias regimes separately and attributes fixed scalar inequalities to exact finite arithmetic certificates included with the manuscript.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The input bits are independent and uniform. Arbitrary output bias means the summary may be unbalanced; it does not mean the theorem permits arbitrary nonuniform input distributions.

The summary is binary. Multi-bit compression, correlated input noise, and other channels require separate statements. Nor is the bound a universal claim that a coordinate optimizes every conceivable accuracy or stability criterion.

M1’s sharpness is at fixed initial information over randomized binary channels. Determining all optimizers under additional fixed-bias constraints is a different question, and the manuscript does not claim every biased Boolean source reaches its refined upper curve.

8. Sources and further reading

M1 states the soft-channel theorem, Boolean refinement, and entropy-production comparison. M2 defines the Hellinger affinity interpretation and its implication to Courtade–Kumar. The original conjecture papers and the differential-method sources linked above provide the main historical path without requiring their technical details to follow the claims.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, Sharp binary-information contraction on the discrete cube (September 24, 2026).
  • M2. OpenAI, Hellinger contraction with arbitrary Boolean output bias (September 24, 2026).

Sources consulted on 9 October 2026 at repository revision fd4aeeb. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: Almost-linear-time exact matching in general graphs
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 120 · Theoretical computer science
Importance 4/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-09

A matching pairs vertices without using any vertex twice. Finding a largest matching has been a cornerstone of graph algorithms since the development of blossom methods. Family 120 claims that an exact maximum matching in a general graph can be found in time almost proportional to the input size, with constant success probability and an execution-time bound that includes unsuccessful random runs.

1. The question

Suppose edges record compatible pairs of objects. We want to choose as many disjoint pairs as possible. Greedily choosing an available edge can get stuck too early: on a path with four vertices, choosing its middle edge gives only one pair, whereas choosing the two outside edges gives two.

A matching to which no edge can simply be added is maximal. A matching with the largest possible number of edges is maximum. The theorem concerns the latter, more demanding objective.

General graphs contain odd cycles, unlike bipartite graphs, whose vertices split into two parts with every edge crossing between them. Odd cycles complicate the exchanges used to enlarge a matching.

The manuscript claims an algorithm taking (n+m)1+o(1)(n+m)^{1+o(1)}(n+m)1+o(1) word operations for nnn vertices and mmm edges. It must return the actual matching edges, not just the optimum’s numerical size.

2. Background and essential definitions

Alternating paths and blossoms

Relative to a current matching, an alternating path uses unmatched and matched edges in turn. If it begins and ends at unmatched vertices, switching the chosen status of its edges increases the matching size by one. Such a path is augmenting.

In bipartite graphs, searching for augmenting paths has a relatively direct layered structure. In general graphs, an alternating search can encounter an odd cycle. Blossom algorithms contract suitable odd structures, continue the search in a smaller representation, and later expand them to recover a valid matching.

A related notion is a factor-critical set: after deleting any prescribed vertex from that set, its remaining vertices have a perfect matching. It can therefore expose different vertices to connect with the rest of the graph while pairing all its other vertices internally.

Input size and almost-linear time

The input graph is simple, undirected, and unweighted. Its adjacency lists contain two neighbor occurrences per edge, together with boundaries for the vertex lists. Isolated vertices count toward the input size.

Put p=n+mp=n+mp=n+m. Almost-linear time means a bound

Cp1+η(p),η(p)⟶0.C p^{1+\eta(p)},\qquad \eta(p)\longrightarrow0.Cp1+η(p),η(p)⟶0.

This is close to linear at the exponent level. It does not necessarily mean O(plog⁡cp)O(p\log^c p)O(plogcp) for a fixed ccc, which is a stronger and more specific kind of bound.

The computational model is a word-RAM with words of O(log⁡(n+2))O(\log(n+2))O(log(n+2)) bits. Basic operations on such words have unit cost. Longer arithmetic, random-bit generation, data movement, initialization, and writing the output are charged.

Prescribed-degree subgraphs

An fff-factor is a spanning subgraph in which each vertex vvv has a prescribed degree f(v)f(v)f(v). “Spanning” means it keeps every vertex, though some may have prescribed degree zero.

Perfect matching is the case f(v)=1f(v)=1f(v)=1 everywhere. More general prescriptions ask for several incident edges at some vertices, subject to the edges actually available in the host graph.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Hall’s theorem characterizes complete pairing on one side of a bipartite graph. Tutte’s theorem identifies the additional odd-component obstruction in general graphs. These existence results reveal the structures algorithms must manage.

Edmonds’s blossom algorithm made general-graph matching polynomial-time. His matching-polytope description also explains why vertex-degree constraints alone are insufficient: assigning one half to every edge of a triangle satisfies those constraints but has total fractional size one and a half, whereas an integral matching has size at most one.

Hopcroft and Karp accelerated bipartite matching by finding many shortest augmenting paths in phases. The Micali–Vazirani algorithm extended the square-root-times-edges scale to general graphs, conventionally O(mn)O(m\sqrt n)O(mn​), with input-reading costs included when needed.

Algebraic methods provide a different route. Randomized evaluations of the Tutte matrix connect matching with linear algebra. Mucha and Sankowski and Harvey developed algorithms producing explicit maximum matchings at the matrix-multiplication time scale. Such bounds are especially relevant for dense graphs.

For bipartite graphs, exact matching reduces to integral flow. Almost-linear flow algorithms, including the deterministic minimum-cost flow result of van den Brand and collaborators, consequently yield almost-linear bipartite matching.

The remaining challenge addressed here is the general graph: retain the efficiency of modern flow and continuous-optimization machinery while handling odd blocks and recovering explicit edges. M1 incorporates that structure rather than assuming a bipartite reduction with no overhead or loss.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

M1 states that one uniform randomized word-RAM algorithm halts on every computation path within

C(n+m)1+η(n+m)C(n+m)^{1+\eta(n+m)}C(n+m)1+η(n+m)

instructions, for a nonincreasing function η\etaη tending to zero. With probability at least 2/32/32/3, it outputs a list of edges forming a maximum-cardinality matching.

A perfect matching is not promised. The graph may be disconnected and contain isolated vertices, and adjacency lists may appear in any valid order.

On graphs with m=O(n)m=O(n)m=O(n), the bound is n1+o(1)n^{1+o(1)}n1+o(1). At the dense extreme m=Θ(n2)m=\Theta(n^2)m=Θ(n2), it is n2+o(1)n^{2+o(1)}n2+o(1). The same finite algorithm and exponent envelope cover the whole density range.

The paper also claims the same almost-linear time and success probability for deciding whether an fff-factor exists and returning it when it does. The supplied degrees satisfy 0≤f(v)≤deg⁡G(v)0\le f(v)\le\deg_G(v)0≤f(v)≤degG​(v) and fit in ordinary machine words.

“Exact” refers to the optimum attained on successful runs. The algorithm is randomized and may fail with the stated probability; exact optimization is not synonymous with deterministic certainty.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 4/5, provisional. Maximum matching is a fundamental polynomial-time optimization problem. An almost-linear algorithm across all graph densities would substantially narrow the asymptotic distance between reading the input and solving it exactly.

The sparse case is particularly significant. A bound expressed only through matrix multiplication may spend far more than linear time even when the graph has few edges. The claimed input-size guarantee responds to actual sparsity.

The fff-factor consequence broadens the result to prescribed-degree design problems. Its reduction must preserve a compact instance and recover a concrete subgraph, so it is more informative than an abstract equivalence of decision problems.

The claim is an asymptotic complexity advance, not a benchmark for a usable matching library. It also concerns cardinality; arbitrary maximum-weight matching is a separate objective.

6. The main idea

Reduce to a manageable exact subproblem

The paper’s central procedure finds perfect matchings in graphs of maximum degree three. Reductions convert general cardinality questions to this task while retaining identifiers that allow returned edges to be decoded into the original graph.

Bounding degree limits local complexity. The reductions must also limit total size; replacing a vertex by a huge gadget would erase the intended running-time improvement.

Store odd blocks without repeatedly opening them

The matching state groups some vertices into odd factor-critical blocks. Each block carries information about an internal matching with any designated vertex exposed. Outside vertices can be assigned to blocks through original edges.

This allows the algorithm to change how a block connects externally without rebuilding its entire internal matching immediately. It extends the basic contraction-and-expansion idea with a representation designed for frequent local updates.

The difficulty is that structural changes can invalidate assignments. Repairing every affected structure by scanning all its vertices would be too expensive.

Let accumulated imbalance pay for repairs

The construction maintains several allocation records at different margins. A record distributes available contributions among neighboring blocks; its residual describes remaining capacity. A nonnegative debt allows a temporary failure of the desired margin.

When a repair starts, it explores only blocks with enough debt relative to their size. Exact flow computations either repair the allocation or identify a collection of blocks to remove from that state. The bookkeeping ensures that useful progress or a decrease in debt pays for the amount of structure examined.

This is an amortized analysis: one operation may be costly, but repeated costly operations require a resource that cannot be spent indefinitely. The paper makes the resource explicit across several scales of constraints.

Search for improvement in compressed representations

The optimization procedure seeks circulation directions that give sufficient progress relative to weighted length. A circulation is an assignment of directed edge flows with no net accumulation at vertices.

Dynamic forests and routing summaries represent long paths compactly. The algorithm tracks both signed coordinate changes and total absolute motion, because opposite movements may cancel algebraically while still costing computation.

A hierarchy of routing structures preserves these quantities as representations change. Finally, schedules over fixed-parameter procedures produce one uniform algorithm with a common exponent tending to one. This last step matters: a separate algorithm for each desired exponent slack would be a different assertion.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The headline theorem assumes a simple unweighted graph explicitly stored by adjacency lists. It does not assert the same bound for compressed graph descriptions, arbitrary edge weights, or every model of accessing a graph.

Its time bound holds on every random path, while its correctness guarantee is probabilistic. The stated 2/32/32/3 success probability should not be silently replaced by certainty or by a stronger high-probability claim.

The o(1)o(1)o(1) exponent does not specify a small practical overhead. Constants, thresholds, and the cost of sophisticated dynamic structures remain relevant to implementation.

The natural further directions include deterministic general-graph matching at comparable complexity, simpler explicit overheads, and corresponding results for weighted objectives. They are separate from the family theorem.

8. Sources and further reading

M1’s Theorem 1.1 fixes the input representation, machine operations, success probability, and uniformity. Its final section states the prescribed-degree consequence. The classical matching and modern flow papers linked above explain the combination of odd-set structure and efficient continuous optimization that motivates the construction.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, Almost-Linear-Time Maximum-Cardinality Matching in General Graphs (September 24, 2026).

Sources consulted on 9 October 2026 at repository revision fd4aeeb. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: Almost-linear expected-time approximation of edit distance
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 121 · Theoretical computer science
Importance 4/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-09

Edit distance measures how many insertions, deletions, and substitutions turn one string into another. Its familiar dynamic program examines a quadratic grid of possibilities. Family 121 claims that, for any fixed requested multiplicative accuracy, a randomized algorithm can estimate the distance in almost-linear expected time.
