entry.title: Quasipolynomial algorithms for mean-payoff, stochastic and parity games
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 104 · Theoretical computer science
Importance 4/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-08

A game can have finitely many positions but continue forever. One player wants a good average reward; the other tries to keep that average low. Family 104 claims algorithms for solving such games in quasipolynomial time, measured in the entire binary input length. This last qualification is central: a reward of enormous magnitude can have a short description, so an algorithm must avoid spending time proportional to the reward itself.

1. The question

Imagine a controller operating a system indefinitely. Some transitions earn resources, while others consume them. The controller chooses certain moves; an adversarial environment chooses the rest. From which starting states can the controller guarantee a nonnegative long-run average?

Two natural extensions complicate the question. Some transitions may be random, so performance is measured in expectation. Alternatively, the controller may need both a satisfactory average and a recurring logical obligation, such as returning to a designated kind of state infinitely often.

The family studies ordinary mean-payoff games and these two separate extensions. Its four manuscripts claim a deterministic quasipolynomial bound for each relevant winning-set problem, along with stronger value and strategy outputs for the ordinary model.

2. Background and essential definitions

Infinite plays on a finite graph

An arena is a finite directed graph whose vertices are assigned to two players, Max and Min. Each vertex has an outgoing edge. The owner of the current vertex chooses the next edge, producing an infinite sequence e0,e1,…e_0,e_1,\ldotse0​,e1​,…. Each edge has an integer reward w(e)w(e)w(e).

The payoff is the lower limiting average

MP⁡(π)=lim inf⁡T→∞1T∑t=0T−1w(et).\operatorname{MP}(\pi)=\liminf_{T\to\infty}\frac1T\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}w(e_t).MP(π)=T→∞liminf​T1​t=0∑T−1​w(et​).

The notation lim inf⁡\liminfliminf handles averages that oscillate rather than converge: it records their eventual lower level. Max wants this payoff large, and Min wants it small. Repeating a two-edge cycle with rewards +3+3+3 and −1-1−1 gives mean payoff 111, regardless of any finite initial route into the cycle.

A strategy tells a player how to move after every possible history. A positional strategy remembers only the current vertex. In ordinary finite mean-payoff games, optimal positional strategies exist for both players, even though general strategies are allowed. The value at a vertex is the payoff Max can guarantee against Min’s best opposition.

Chance and parity are different additions

In a stochastic game, some vertices belong to Chance. At those vertices, the next edge is selected according to an explicitly given rational probability distribution. The claimed stochastic result uses

val⁡(v)=sup⁡σinf⁡τEv,σ,τ[MP⁡(π)],\operatorname{val}(v)=\sup_\sigma\inf_\tau\mathbb E_{v,\sigma,\tau}[\operatorname{MP}(\pi)],val(v)=σsup​τinf​Ev,σ,τ​[MP(π)],

where σ\sigmaσ and τ\tauτ are the players’ strategies. The expectation is taken after the pathwise lower limit. A nonnegative expected payoff need not mean a nonnegative payoff on every play.

In the parity extension, each vertex instead carries a nonnegative integer called its priority. Under the paper’s convention, the least priority appearing infinitely often must be even. If priorities 2 and 5 recur forever, the condition succeeds; if 3 and 4 recur forever, it fails. A priority visited only finitely often does not affect the outcome.

Max must satisfy both parity and nonnegative mean payoff on every play allowed by the opponent. This combined objective is more demanding than either condition separately.

The size of a number is not its value

An integer of magnitude 2b2^b2b needs only about bbb binary digits. A runtime proportional to that integer is exponential in its encoding length. Algorithms polynomial in numerical magnitudes, such as the largest reward WWW, are called pseudopolynomial when this dependence prevents a polynomial bound in the input length.

Write LLL for the complete binary input length, including the graph, ownership, rewards, probabilities, and priorities that the model uses. The claimed common bound is

2O((log⁡(L+2))2)=(L+2)O(log⁡(L+2)).2^{O((\log(L+2))^2)}=(L+2)^{O(\log(L+2))}.2O((log(L+2))2)=(L+2)O(log(L+2)).

This is quasipolynomial: larger than a fixed-degree polynomial in general, but much smaller asymptotically than 2cL2^{cL}2cL for a fixed positive ccc. A bit-operation bound counts the cost of manipulating numerical data rather than treating arithmetic on arbitrarily large integers as free.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Shapley’s 1953 work introduced stochastic games, and subsequent research developed long-run average objectives. Ehrenfeucht and Mycielski’s 1979 theorem established the positional structure of ordinary mean-payoff games. Finite strategy descriptions became available even though plays are infinite.

Zwick and Paterson in 1996 developed complexity connections and pseudopolynomial algorithms for mean-payoff games. Later energy-game methods used vertex potentials and progress measures. An energy objective asks whether an initial credit can keep every finite accumulated total nonnegative; this is closely related to, but distinct from, a nonnegative limiting average. The numerical reward dependence remained a central obstacle to bounds in binary input length.

Parity games saw a major breakthrough in 2017 when Calude, Jain, Khoussainov, Li, and Stephan obtained a quasipolynomial algorithm. Parity games reduce to mean-payoff games, but a reduction in that direction does not turn a parity solver into a solver for arbitrary mean-payoff games.

For the combined objective, Chatterjee, Henzinger, and Jurdziński introduced mean-payoff parity games in 2005. Daviaud, Jurdziński, and Lazić in 2018 replaced an exponential priority dependence by a quasipolynomial one. Their bound still retained a numerical weight factor, hence the description “pseudo-quasipolynomial.”

Stochastic games formed another longstanding line. Condon’s 1992 work placed the simple stochastic game threshold problem in NP∩coNP\mathsf{NP}\cap\mathsf{coNP}NP∩coNP, meaning both yes- and no-instances have polynomially checkable certificates. Subexponential algorithms and results for restricted arenas followed, but these did not supply the general deterministic quasipolynomial binary-length bound claimed here.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

All bounds below count the full explicit binary input. Large signed rewards are allowed; the stochastic paper also allows arbitrary rational chance probabilities, and the parity paper allows unrestricted binary priorities.

ManuscriptModelClaimed output
Deterministic algorithmOrdinary mean-payoffAll nonnegative-value starts; also exact rational values and optimal positional strategies
Randomized algorithmOrdinary mean-payoffThe full winning set with success probability at least 7/87/87/8, with a checkable-output variant
Stochastic algorithmMean payoff with Chance verticesAll starts with nonnegative expectation-of-liminf value, including value zero
Parity algorithmMean payoff conjoined with parityAll starts from which Max can force both conditions

The deterministic, stochastic, and parity algorithms claim the quasipolynomial bound displayed above. The randomized algorithm claims that bound on every random tape, including unsuccessful runs. Its probability guarantee covers the whole returned set, not merely one vertex at a time.

The randomized manuscript also states a polynomial-time procedure that checks the produced winning regions and positional strategies or reports failure. Repeating until this check succeeds gives an always-correct randomized algorithm with the same form of expected quasipolynomial bound. This certificate check is part of the paper’s algorithmic claim.

The deterministic ordinary-game manuscript obtains exact values and globally optimal positional strategies through further winning-set queries. Those stronger outputs should not be silently assigned to the two extension papers, whose headline theorems compute threshold sets.

5. Why the advance matters

The gain is especially meaningful when rewards or probability denominators are large. A number such as 210002^{1000}21000 has a manageable binary description; enumerating values up to it is not manageable. A bound in LLL explicitly addresses this mismatch.

The stochastic claim also reaches simple stochastic reachability games. Make the target absorbing with reward +1+1+1, and give other transitions reward −1-1−1. A play that eventually reaches the target has limiting average +1+1+1; one that never reaches it has average −1-1−1. Therefore

E[MP⁡]=2Pr⁡[target is reached]−1.\mathbb E[\operatorname{MP}]=2\Pr[\text{target is reached}]-1.E[MP]=2Pr[target is reached]−1.

Testing nonnegative value then answers whether the optimal worst-case reachability probability is at least one half. The stochastic manuscript explicitly gives this reduction.

Importance: 4/5, provisional. A common quasipolynomial bound for these longstanding graph-game problems would be a major algorithmic advance, with consequences for models used in verification and control. A polynomial-time bound would be a further step beyond the claims here.

6. The main idea

Change potentials without changing long-run rewards

Assign a number h(v)h(v)h(v), called a potential, to each vertex. Replace an edge reward by

wh(u,v)=w(u,v)+h(v)−h(u).w_h(u,v)=w(u,v)+h(v)-h(u).wh​(u,v)=w(u,v)+h(v)−h(u).

Along a path, the potential terms telescope to the difference between the final and initial potentials. Since there are finitely many vertices, that difference divided by the path length tends to zero. Cycle sums and long-run averages are preserved.

Potentials can therefore reorganize the local inequalities that reveal winning behavior. The ordinary-game algorithms work with integer vectors in finite boxes and compare them with suitable lower and upper bounds on these inequalities. A naive iteration might move through a box one numerical unit at a time, making it too slow when rewards are large.

The deterministic paper instead recursively narrows boxes and assigns positive masses to coordinates. These masses track which potential comparisons must remain valid. Most recursive children increase a progress measure by a fixed factor; at most one child preserves it while reducing the box width. Only logarithmically many branching progress steps can occur along a path. Counting their possible positions yields the claimed quasipolynomial recursion size.

This is an algorithm for extracting the necessary boundary information without enumerating every possible potential value.

Discount the stochastic game, but avoid slow iteration

For the stochastic extension, the paper first studies a discounted reward operator. With 0<u<10<u<10<u<1, an edge to vertex jjj contributes

u w(e)+(1−u)tj,u\,w(e)+(1-u)t_j,uw(e)+(1−u)tj​,

followed by a maximum, minimum, or probability-weighted average according to the vertex owner. Discounting gives a unique fixed point.

The manuscript supplies a sufficiently small discount and a lower bound on the magnitude of nonzero game values. Together these turn a sufficiently accurate fixed-point estimate into an exact sign decision, including zero. But ordinary fixed-point iteration can require time proportional to the inverse discount. The proposed recursive comparison method uses monotonicity and the operator’s behavior under common shifts to avoid that numerical dependence.

Combine long-run reward with repeated obligations

For parity, the algorithm recursively studies regions where a player can stay and win, called dominions, using the ordinary mean-payoff solver as a subroutine. Controlling the number of recursive calls is only part of the challenge: switching among individually successful strategies can repeatedly incur startup costs.

The paper handles this by controlling finite-prefix losses and scheduling increasingly long reward phases between parity visits. If reward phases have lengths 1,2,3,…1,2,3,\ldots1,2,3,…, then after kkk phases the useful time grows quadratically in kkk, while a bounded cost per intervening visit grows only linearly. Thus the average overhead can vanish while the required priority is still visited infinitely often. The actual construction also accounts for adversarial choices and restarts.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The two extensions are separate. The family does not, through these statements alone, provide the same theorem for games combining stochastic transitions, mean payoff, and parity simultaneously.

The stochastic objective is nonnegative expected pathwise liminf payoff. It is not an almost-sure guarantee of nonnegative payoff, nor should expectation and the lower limit be interchanged without justification.

The positional strategies in the ordinary-game result do not imply that a player enforcing the parity conjunction can always use finite memory. Earlier work shows that infinite memory can be needed for that combined objective. The increasing-phase idea explains why memory may matter.

Finally, quasipolynomial time is still an asymptotic upper bound, not a practical benchmark or a polynomial-time solution. Whether stronger general bounds are possible, and how these methods compare with existing solvers on realistic arenas, remain separate questions.

8. Sources and further reading

The four manuscripts are credited to OpenAI:

  1. Deterministic quasipolynomial-time mean-payoff games — September 25, 2026; Theorem 1.1 and Section 7.
  2. Randomized quasipolynomial-time mean-payoff games — September 25, 2026; Theorem 1.1 and Corollary 8.1.
  3. Turn-Based Stochastic Mean-Payoff Games in Deterministic Quasipolynomial Time — October 5, 2026; Theorem 1.1.
  4. Mean-payoff parity games in quasipolynomial time — October 5, 2026; Theorem 1.1.

Historical sources are linked in Section 3. Optional background: mean-payoff games, parity games, and pseudopolynomial time.

entry.title: Derandomization of logarithmic space — L = RL = BPL
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 103 · Theoretical computer science
Importance 5/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-08

A computer can inspect a large input while retaining very little working memory. Randomness often helps such a machine explore possibilities without storing its history. Family 103 claims that, for polynomial-time decisions with bounded error, random bits add no power when working memory is logarithmic in the input length. The proposed simulation removes randomness while preserving that stringent memory bound.

1. The question

Imagine navigating a large network while remembering only your current location and a few counters. You cannot store the set of places already visited. A random walk offers a natural strategy: repeatedly choose a neighboring vertex and hope eventually to reach the destination.

More generally, a small-memory program may read fresh random bits to choose its next action. If it usually gives the correct answer, can a deterministic program always give that answer using the same order of memory and still finish in polynomial time?

The claimed equality

L=RL=BPL\mathsf L=\mathsf{RL}=\mathsf{BPL}L=RL=BPL

answers yes for the standard bounded-error logarithmic-space model. The letters name classes of decision problems, which will be defined below. This is a statement about computation under a simultaneous time and memory constraint.

2. Background and essential definitions

Why logarithmic memory is so restrictive

For an input of length nnn, an integer identifying one input position requires about log⁡2n\log_2 nlog2​n bits. Thus O(log⁡n)O(\log n)O(logn) memory holds a fixed number of positions, counters, or similarly sized quantities. It cannot hold a list of nnn visited vertices.

The input is on a read-only tape and is not charged to working memory. The machine may revisit it. Everything writable that remains in use does count, including temporary numerical values and the information needed to resume a suspended subroutine. An output tape, when used, is write-only.

A configuration records the machine’s state, head positions, and work-tape contents. A fixed machine using O(log⁡n)O(\log n)O(logn) bits has only polynomially many possible configurations. If a deterministic machine halts, it cannot revisit the same complete configuration: doing so would repeat the same future forever. Consequently, a halting deterministic log-space machine also has a polynomial running-time bound.

Three classes of decisions

A language is a set of finite input strings; deciding it means answering whether a given string belongs to the set. The classes in the title have these meanings:

ClassRandomness and errorWorking memory
L\mathsf LLDeterministic, always correctO(log⁡n)O(\log n)O(logn)
RL\mathsf{RL}RLNever accepts a no-instance; accepts a yes-instance with probability at least 1/21/21/2O(log⁡n)O(\log n)O(logn)
BPL\mathsf{BPL}BPLAccepts a no-instance with probability at most 1/31/31/3, a yes-instance with probability at least 2/32/32/3O(log⁡n)O(\log n)O(logn)

The randomized machines must run in polynomial time on every sequence of random bits. Their coins are fresh independent fair bits. The error bounds are per input, not averages over a distribution of inputs.

The particular constants are conventional. For example, a one-sided algorithm can be repeated a constant number of times, accepting if any run accepts, to reduce its failure probability. The repetitions reuse memory. It follows that

L⊆RL⊆BPL.\mathsf L\subseteq\mathsf{RL}\subseteq\mathsf{BPL}.L⊆RL⊆BPL.

The difficult direction is the reverse containment: removing randomness from an arbitrary two-sided bounded-error computation.

Why trying every random tape is not enough

A computation using RRR random bits has 2R2^R2R possible random tapes. If RRR is polynomial in nnn, listing all tapes takes exponential time, and even storing the current tape index can exceed logarithmic memory.

A pseudorandom generator replaces those tapes by outputs derived from short seeds. The outputs need only look random to the restricted class of computations being simulated. A seed of length clog⁡nc\log nclogn, for fixed ccc, has only ncn^cnc possibilities. A seed of length (log⁡n)2(\log n)^2(logn)2 has nlog⁡nn^{\log n}nlogn possibilities, already beyond polynomial time. The difference between one logarithm and two therefore has major consequences.

3. Development history and previous partial results

In 1979, Aleliunas, Karp, Lipton, Lovász, and Rackoff showed how random walks solve undirected connectivity with little memory. This gave a concrete example of the broader question: was randomness essential, or merely a convenient way to explore a graph?

Nisan’s 1992 generator supplied short pseudorandom sequences for space-bounded computations. For space SSS and RRR random bits, its seed length is O(Slog⁡R)O(S\log R)O(SlogR). With logarithmic space and polynomially many random bits, this becomes O((log⁡n)2)O((\log n)^2)O((logn)2). Enumerating all seeds gives a useful deterministic simulation, but not the desired polynomial-time, logarithmic-space combination. Nisan’s later simultaneous simulation obtained polynomial time with squared-logarithmic space.

Saks and Zhou reduced the deterministic space needed for general bounded-error log-space computation to O((log⁡n)3/2)O((\log n)^{3/2})O((logn)3/2). Hoza’s 2021 work improved that space bound to

O ⁣((log⁡n)3/2log⁡log⁡n).O\!\left(\frac{(\log n)^{3/2}}{\sqrt{\log\log n}}\right).O(loglogn​(logn)3/2​).

These are advances toward the memory target. A smaller-space simulation and a simulation with a simultaneous polynomial-time guarantee are different accomplishments; one should not silently attach the latter guarantee to every space-containment theorem.

Reingold’s undirected connectivity algorithm, presented in 2005 and published in journal form in 2008, reached deterministic logarithmic space for the original random-walk example. But undirected graphs possess symmetry absent from general computation graphs. Solving that special case did not settle arbitrary randomized log-space computation.

Family 103 claims to reach the full target: deterministic logarithmic space and polynomial time for all machines in the bounded-error model. It also describes a compiler that constructs the deterministic simulator from a randomized program with supplied resource bounds.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

The family consists of one manuscript. Theorem 1.1 states the class equality in the title. Its quantitative foundation is Theorem 1.2, concerning acceptance probabilities even when no yes/no probability gap is promised.

Fix a polynomial-time randomized log-space machine MMM. Let pM(x)p_M(x)pM​(x) be the probability that it accepts input xxx, whose length is nnn. Given an accuracy parameter q≥1q\ge1q≥1, the claimed deterministic algorithm outputs a dyadic rational p^\widehat pp​, meaning a rational with a power-of-two denominator, such that

∣p^−pM(x)∣≤2−q.|\widehat p-p_M(x)|\le2^{-q}.∣p​−pM​(x)∣≤2−q.

The stated resources are

work space=O(log⁡(n+2)+q),time=(n+2)O(1)2O(q).\begin{aligned}\text{work space}&=O(\log(n+2)+q),\\\text{time}&=(n+2)^{O(1)}2^{O(q)}.\end{aligned}work spacetime​=O(log(n+2)+q),=(n+2)O(1)2O(q).​

The parameter is supplied in unary as 1q1^q1q, a string of qqq ones. The constants may depend on the fixed source machine.

For q=3q=3q=3, the error is at most 1/81/81/8, smaller than the distance 1/61/61/6 between either bounded-error threshold and 1/21/21/2. Comparing the estimate with 1/21/21/2 therefore gives an exact decision. Taking qqq proportional to log⁡n\log nlogn yields inverse-polynomial accuracy while retaining logarithmic space and polynomial time.

Theorem 13.1 adds effectivity: given a source machine and supplied polynomial-time and logarithmic-space bounds, one terminating compiler produces a deterministic decider together with explicit resource bounds. The compiler assumes the source satisfies the supplied bounds; it does not decide that property for arbitrary programs.

5. Why the advance matters

Randomness and memory can substitute for each other. A random walk avoids recording an elaborate route; a deterministic search often remembers more of its progress. The claimed result would show that this apparent advantage of randomness disappears at the level of log-space decision classes, even while retaining polynomial time.

The probability-estimation statement also goes beyond saying that some deterministic decider exists. It offers a common numerical task from which many decisions follow. When a computation’s acceptance probability is separated from a threshold by an inverse-polynomial margin, a sufficiently accurate estimate can decide which side it lies on.

Importance: 5/5, provisional. An equality of these central complexity classes would resolve a longstanding general derandomization problem, encompassing many algorithms rather than a single application. The score reflects that breadth, not a claim that the resulting simulation is immediately practical.

6. The main idea

Turn the computation into linear algebra

Attach a time coordinate to each configuration. Every transition then moves forward, so the configuration graph has no directed cycle. Let SSS be its transition matrix, with accepting terminal states represented by a vector eee. Rows of SSS have nonnegative entries summing to at most one; missing probability corresponds to stopping.

Because a polynomial time bound limits the number of layers, some power ST+1S^{T+1}ST+1 is zero. The acceptance-probability vector can be expressed as

p=(I−S)−1e=(I+S+S2+⋯+ST)e,p=(I-S)^{-1}e=(I+S+S^2+\cdots+S^T)e,p=(I−S)−1e=(I+S+S2+⋯+ST)e,

where III is the identity matrix. Each power accounts for paths of a particular length. This makes the target precise, but storing even one full vector would exceed the memory budget.

Estimate individual quantities and recompute the rest

The proposed algorithm therefore treats matrices and vectors as quantities whose entries can be generated when needed. A hierarchy of corrections and configuration copies moves probability contributions into accumulated rewards, while controlling the transitions that remain. It estimates entries through sparse descriptions rather than maintaining complete arrays.

The difficult resource is everything that stays live during recursion. If each of log⁡n\log nlogn nested calls saved a configuration address of log⁡n\log nlogn bits, the stack alone would use squared-logarithmic space. The manuscript uses short fingerprints to compare addresses, recomputes information that would otherwise be saved, and requests numerical values one digit at a time.

Its memory accounting assigns a decreasing allowance to recursive calls. A parent’s retained data are charged to the allowance lost when descending to its child. Such differences can telescope along the active call chain, bounding the total rather than bounding each call separately. This is the claimed mechanism for avoiding a hidden extra logarithm.

Enumerate a small family of estimates

The construction uses a finite family of environments described with O(log⁡n)O(\log n)O(logn) bits. More than three quarters of the relevant estimates are claimed to be accurate, and every estimate can be evaluated by a halting deterministic log-space procedure, including inaccurate ones.

There are only polynomially many descriptions. The final algorithm enumerates them and finds a median by repeated scans, retaining counters and current candidates instead of sorting a stored list. If most estimates lie within a prescribed interval around the truth, so does their median.

This explains how randomness can enter the analysis without appearing in the final machine. A probabilistic argument establishes that enough members of a small family work; exhaustive deterministic processing of that family extracts the answer. The paper’s main technical burden is constructing the family and evaluating each member within the memory budget.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

“Exact” refers to the resulting decisions and the logarithmic order of the space bound. It does not mean every acceptance probability is output as its exact rational expansion. Greater numerical precision costs additional memory and time according to the displayed bounds.

The result concerns polynomial-time computations with fresh random bits and logarithmic working space. It does not assert P=BPP\mathsf P=\mathsf{BPP}P=BPP, the analogous general polynomial-time derandomization statement without this memory restriction. Nor does it give a deterministic solution to every problem in NP\mathsf{NP}NP.

The input may be reread. Consequently, the theorem is not automatically a one-pass streaming algorithm for data that cannot be revisited. Similarly, an arbitrary reusable random tape is a different computational model from a stream of fresh independent bits.

Polynomial time permits large exponents and constants depending on the source machine. The compiler’s explicit bounds establish a theoretical resource guarantee; obtaining a practical implementation with competitive running time is a separate question. The claimed result addresses whether randomness increases decision power under these constraints, not whether removing it is always a good engineering choice.

8. Sources and further reading

Exact Derandomization of Logarithmic Space: L = RL = BPL, credited to OpenAI, September 23, 2026. Theorems 1.1–1.2 state the main claims; Section 1.2 explains the construction; Theorem 13.1 gives the compiler statement.

The historical papers are linked in Section 3. Optional background: space complexity, randomized algorithms, and pseudorandom generators in complexity theory.

entry.title: The Unique Games Conjecture and optimal approximation thresholds
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 102 · Theoretical computer science
Importance 5/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-08

An optimization problem can be too hard to solve exactly and still admit useful approximate answers. The difficult question is how close an efficient algorithm can always get. Family 102 claims a resolution of the Unique Games Conjecture and sharp approximation barriers for several familiar graph problems. Its central theme is that a locally simple rule can conceal a globally difficult choice.

1. The question

Suppose a network’s vertices must receive labels. Each edge specifies a rule translating the label at one endpoint into the required label at the other. Once one endpoint’s label is known, there is exactly one acceptable reply. Nevertheless, cycles can impose conflicting requirements.

Can an efficient algorithm distinguish a network in which almost every rule can be obeyed from one in which every labeling violates almost all rules? The Unique Games Conjecture predicts that this distinction is computationally hard, for a sufficiently large but fixed set of labels.

This sounds specialized. Its importance comes from reductions: procedures that transform one computational problem into another while preserving the distinction between good and bad solutions. Unique Games became a common starting point for predicting the best possible approximation guarantees across many optimization problems.

2. Background and essential definitions

Labels, constraints, and value

Let KKK be a finite set of labels. A constraint on an oriented edge e=(u,v)e=(u,v)e=(u,v) specifies a permutation πe:K→K\pi_e:K\to Kπe​:K→K, a rearrangement with no repetitions. A labeling aaa satisfies this edge when

a(v)=πe(a(u)).a(v)=\pi_e(a(u)).a(v)=πe​(a(u)).

For example, with labels 0,1,20,1,20,1,2, an edge might require the second label to be the first plus one, modulo three. Three such rules around a triangle are consistent; changing just one of them can make the cycle inconsistent. “Unique” describes the permitted reply on an edge, not the number of global solutions.

The value of an instance GGG is the best fraction of constraints that can be satisfied:

val⁡(G)=max⁡a#{constraints satisfied by a}#{constraints}.\operatorname{val}(G)=\max_a\frac{\#\{\text{constraints satisfied by }a\}}{\#\{\text{constraints}\}}.val(G)=amax​#{constraints}#{constraints satisfied by a}​.

A gap problem promises that this value lies either above a high threshold or below a low threshold. No answer is required for the intermediate cases. The high threshold is called completeness; the low threshold is called soundness. These names describe the reduction’s mathematical guarantees.

What computational hardness means

A polynomial-time algorithm takes at most ncn^cnc steps for some fixed exponent ccc, up to constant factors, on an input of length nnn. This is the usual theoretical meaning of efficient. The class P\mathsf PP contains decision problems with such algorithms; NP\mathsf{NP}NP contains problems whose proposed yes-answers have efficiently checkable certificates.

In 3SAT, the input is an AND of clauses, each an OR of three Boolean literals. The question is whether some truth assignment satisfies every clause. A polynomial-time reduction from 3SAT establishes NP-hardness. An efficient algorithm solving the target problem would then imply P=NP\mathsf P=\mathsf{NP}P=NP.

For a maximization problem, an α\alphaα-approximation returns a feasible solution worth at least α\alphaα times the optimum, with 0<α≤10<\alpha\le10<α≤1. Larger ratios are better. For a minimization problem, a CCC-approximation costs at most CCC times the optimum, with C≥1C\ge1C≥1. Smaller factors are better. Confusing these conventions reverses the meaning of a hardness threshold.

3. Development history and previous partial results

The PCP breakthroughs of the early 1990s connected approximation to checking a proof by inspecting only a few locations. Roughly, a valid proof passes the checks, while an invalid claim forces many local failures. Turning those checks into constraints creates a gap between nearly satisfiable and highly unsatisfiable optimization instances. The Arora–Lund–Motwani–Sudan–Szegedy paper is one foundational source.

On the algorithmic side, Goemans and Williamson introduced a geometric method for Max-Cut in 1994, with the journal version appearing in 1995. They replaced the discrete choice of two sides by unit vectors, optimized a semidefinite relaxation, and used a random hyperplane to turn the vectors back into a cut. The resulting guarantee approaches 0.8785670.8785670.878567 of the optimum.

Khot proposed Unique Games in 2002. It offered a particularly simple hardness hypothesis from which precise approximation barriers could follow. Khot, Kindler, Mossel, and O’Donnell related it to the Goemans–Williamson threshold; Khot and Regev obtained the factor-two barrier for Vertex Cover under the same hypothesis. Raghavendra’s 2008 work extended this connection between semidefinite algorithms and conditional hardness to a broad class of constraint satisfaction problems.

The 2017–2018 work on Grassmann graphs and 2-to-2 games was a major partial advance. Its expansion theorem, later published by Khot, Minzer, and Safra, completed the games result with imperfect completeness. It gave stronger unconditional approximation barriers, including Vertex Cover hardness below 2\sqrt22​, and a Unique Games gap with completeness near one half and soundness arbitrarily small. Raising Unique Games completeness from about one half to arbitrarily close to one remained a separate obstacle.

There were also algorithmic advances, including subexponential algorithms for nearly satisfiable Unique Games. Subexponential time can be much smaller than brute force while still exceeding every polynomial bound. Such progress therefore did not settle the polynomial-time hardness question.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

The Unique Games statement

Theorem 1.1 of the first manuscript claims that, for every fixed pair ε,δ∈(0,1/2)\varepsilon,\delta\in(0,1/2)ε,δ∈(0,1/2), a deterministic polynomial-time reduction transforms a 3SAT formula φ\varphiφ into a game GφG_\varphiGφ​ with

φ satisfiable⟹val⁡(Gφ)≥1−ε,φ unsatisfiable⟹val⁡(Gφ)≤δ.\begin{aligned}\varphi\text{ satisfiable}&\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\operatorname{val}(G_\varphi)\ge1-\varepsilon,\\\varphi\text{ unsatisfiable}&\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\operatorname{val}(G_\varphi)\le\delta.\end{aligned}φ satisfiableφ unsatisfiable​⟹val(Gφ​)≥1−ε,⟹val(Gφ​)≤δ.​

The output is a simple, unweighted, bipartite graph. Its alphabet is a finite binary vector space, and each constraint adds a fixed vector to the endpoint label. The alphabet size and the running-time polynomial may depend on the chosen errors, but not on the input formula’s length.

That order matters: first choose the desired constant gap, then choose the alphabet, then handle arbitrarily large formulas. The claim does not provide one small alphabet that works for every possible gap.

Four direct approximation barriers

The other four manuscripts state the following NP-hardness results. Each concerns explicitly represented, unweighted graphs; the first three use simple undirected graphs.

ProblemWhat a solution doesClaimed forbidden guarantee
Max-CutDivide vertices into two sets, maximizing crossing edgesAny fixed ratio above αGW≈0.878567\alpha_{\mathrm{GW}}\approx0.878567αGW​≈0.878567
Vertex CoverChoose vertices meeting every edgeAny fixed factor below 222
Min-UnCutMinimize edges whose endpoints stay on the same sideEvery fixed factor C>1C>1C>1
Directed feedback vertex setDelete vertices until no directed cycle remainsEvery fixed constant factor

The Max-Cut constant can be written as

αGW=min⁡−1≤ρ<12arccos⁡ρπ(1−ρ).\alpha_{\mathrm{GW}}=\min_{-1\le\rho<1}\frac{2\arccos\rho}{\pi(1-\rho)}.αGW​=−1≤ρ<1min​π(1−ρ)2arccosρ​.

Here ρ\rhoρ is the inner product of two unit vectors. The numerator and denominator compare how often a random hyperplane separates those vectors with the value assigned to their edge by the relaxation.

The papers present these as direct reductions using established PCP, Label Cover, and imperfect-completeness game-hardness inputs. They do not use the new Unique Games theorem as a premise. The family thus contains two routes to approximation consequences: the general conjecture claim and separate problem-specific constructions. See Max-Cut, Vertex Cover, Min-UnCut, and directed feedback vertex set.

5. Why the advance matters

The distinction between exact and approximate optimization is substantial. A maximal matching immediately gives a factor-two Vertex Cover: select both endpoints of every matched edge. Every cover must select at least one endpoint per matching edge, and maximality ensures the selected endpoints cover all edges. A fixed improvement below two would therefore improve a very simple general-purpose guarantee. The claimed hardness says such an improvement cannot hold on every input unless P=NP\mathsf P=\mathsf{NP}P=NP.

For Max-Cut, the implication is different: an unusually precise constant emerging from geometry would describe a general computational boundary. The threshold would no longer depend on assuming Unique Games as an additional hardness hypothesis.

Importance: 5/5, provisional. Resolving a central conjecture used throughout approximation theory, together with several longstanding optimization thresholds, would have exceptional breadth. This rating concerns the significance of the stated claims and can be recalibrated as the collection grows.

6. The main idea

Encode a good solution, then recover information from any good answer

A hardness reduction needs two complementary properties. A satisfying source assignment must produce an excellent target solution. Conversely, an unexpectedly good target solution must reveal a source assignment that contradicts the source problem’s soundness guarantee. The second direction must handle arbitrary target solutions, including ones that do not resemble the intended encoding.

The Unique Games manuscript uses matrices over the two-element field F2\mathbb F_2F2​, where addition is modulo two. In an earlier matrix test, the label corresponding to a vector zzz evaluates a matrix MMM as MzMzMz. A rank-one change M↦M+abTM\mapsto M+ab^{\mathsf T}M↦M+abT changes the answer by

(M+abT)z−Mz=a(bTz).(M+ab^{\mathsf T})z-Mz=a(b^{\mathsf T}z).(M+abT)z−Mz=a(bTz).

The scalar bTzb^{\mathsf T}zbTz is often a fair bit, so simply demanding that the answer stay unchanged loses roughly half the good cases. This illustrates the completeness obstacle.

The proposed replacement applies a nonlinear encoding and changes the noise distribution. Intended answers become stable under the new perturbations, while sufficiently many independent linear observations still detect those perturbations. Fourier analysis then connects unexpectedly stable arbitrary answers to the older matrix structure theorem. Further decoding turns that structure into labels for the original constraints.

The conceptual balance is delicate: making noise harmless to every possible answer would also make a bad instance easy to satisfy. It must preserve the intended answers while retaining enough information to constrain all others.

Why the direct constructions differ

The Max-Cut paper uses Boolean functions representing cuts and a correlated test designed to reproduce the geometric threshold. A coordinate is influential when changing it often changes the function’s output. The paper uses a stability theorem to find influential coordinates, then decodes them into compatible source labels.

The Vertex Cover paper instead studies a large independent set, the complement of a small cover. It associates this set with a Lipschitz function, one whose output cannot change too quickly. Derivatives and variance estimates supply short candidate lists of labels. A central requirement is that each list use only information available at its own endpoint of a source constraint.

The Min-UnCut construction analyzes correlations between encoded bits, then converts them into labels without a loss that grows with the alphabet. The directed feedback vertex set construction starts from the topological order of a graph after deletions: in such an order every remaining arc points forward. It turns the order into Boolean functions and extracts incompatible consequences if too few vertices were deleted. These are distinct mechanisms serving the same reduction principle.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

NP-hardness is not itself a proof that P≠NP\mathsf P\ne\mathsf{NP}P=NP. The interpretation “no polynomial-time algorithm” retains that standard assumption. These are worst-case barriers, not predictions that every real network is difficult or that heuristics cannot work well on structured data.

“Every fixed factor below two” also permits improvements that vanish as the graph grows. A guarantee such as 2−1/log⁡n2-1/\log n2−1/logn eventually approaches two; it does not contradict hardness of each fixed 2−ε2-\varepsilon2−ε.

For Min-UnCut, the identity

OPT⁡uncut(G)=∣E∣−MaxCut⁡(G)\operatorname{OPT}_{\mathrm{uncut}}(G)=|E|-\operatorname{MaxCut}(G)OPTuncut​(G)=∣E∣−MaxCut(G)

does not transfer multiplicative approximation ratios. If the optimum cut leaves only one edge uncut, an additive loss of a thousand crossing edges is enormous relative to that one-edge deletion cost. Ordinary bipartiteness testing, which recognizes zero uncut cost, remains easy.

Nor does “unique” imply hardness of satisfying all constraints exactly. In a perfectly satisfiable permutation system, one can try the possible labels at a root and propagate them through a connected component. The claimed hard promise deliberately allows a small positive fraction of unsatisfied constraints in the good case.

8. Sources and further reading

The five manuscripts are credited to OpenAI, dated September 23, 2026:

  1. The Unique Games Theorem — Theorem 1.1; Sections 1.3–1.4 explain the completeness obstacle and construction.
  2. A Direct Proof of Optimal Max-Cut Hardness — Theorems 1.1–1.2.
  3. The Factor-Two Hardness Threshold for Vertex Cover — Theorem 1.1 and Corollary 1.2.
  4. Constant-factor hardness of Min-UnCut — Theorem 1.1.
  5. Constant-factor hardness of directed feedback vertex set — Theorem 1.1.

Historical sources are linked in Section 3. Optional background: approximation algorithms, semidefinite programming, and the Unique Games Conjecture.

Source revision: adc7f1241b42. Sources consulted: October 8, 2026. Citation data: BibTeX.

See the series’ AI declaration for authorship and review status. Back to the family index.

entry.title: The dynamical phase transition in the Sherrington–Kirkpatrick model
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 227 · Probability and statistical mechanics
Importance 4/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-08

A system can have a perfectly well-defined equilibrium distribution and still take an enormous time to reach it. Family 227 studies this gap in a central model of disordered magnetism. Its eight manuscripts claim a transition from logarithmic relaxation time to a critical power law and then to much slower relaxation. Understanding the claim requires care about both the clock and the initial state.

1. The question

Imagine many tiny magnets, each pointing either up or down. Some pairs prefer to agree; others prefer to disagree. These preferences can conflict: three magnets cannot all disagree with each other. Such frustration produces competing configurations rather than a single obvious arrangement.

Allow one magnet at a time to reconsider its direction, with some thermal randomness. How long until the distribution of configurations forgets where it started?

This is a question about mixing time. Knowing which configurations are likely at equilibrium does not tell us how quickly local updates explore them. Family 227 asks how that exploration changes as temperature crosses the spin-glass transition. The precise results discussed below are claims of the linked manuscripts; their scope and limitations are discussed in Section 7.

2. Background and essential definitions

Spins and random interactions

A configuration is a vector σ=(σ1,…,σn)∈{−1,+1}n\sigma=(\sigma_1,\ldots,\sigma_n)\in\{-1,+1\}^nσ=(σ1​,…,σn​)∈{−1,+1}n. For each pair i<ji<ji<j, draw an independent standard Gaussian variable JijJ_{ij}Jij​, meaning a normal variable of mean zero and variance one. These couplings are drawn once and held fixed. They are called the disorder.

Use the interaction score

HJ(σ)=1n∑i<jJijσiσj.H_J(\sigma)=\frac{1}{\sqrt n}\sum_{i<j}J_{ij}\sigma_i\sigma_j.HJ​(σ)=n​1​i<j∑​Jij​σi​σj​.

Positive couplings reward agreement; negative couplings reward disagreement. Every pair interacts, so this is a mean-field model. The normalization keeps the typical total field acting on one spin of order one. With this sign convention, physical energy is −HJ-H_J−HJ​.

At inverse temperature β\betaβ, the equilibrium, or Gibbs, probability is

πJ,β(σ)=eβHJ(σ)ZJ,β,ZJ,β=∑τ∈{−1,+1}neβHJ(τ).\pi_{J,\beta}(\sigma)=\frac{e^{\beta H_J(\sigma)}}{Z_{J,\beta}},\qquadZ_{J,\beta}=\sum_{\tau\in\{-1,+1\}^n}e^{\beta H_J(\tau)}.πJ,β​(σ)=ZJ,β​eβHJ​(σ)​,ZJ,β​=τ∈{−1,+1}n∑​eβHJ​(τ).

The partition function ZJ,βZ_{J,\beta}ZJ,β​ makes the probabilities sum to one. Larger β\betaβ means lower temperature and stronger preference for favorable interactions. Zero external field means no additional term favors up or down spins individually. In this normalization, the critical inverse temperature is β=1\beta=1β=1.

The dynamics and its clock

In heat-bath Glauber dynamics, each spin has an independent clock ringing at rate one. At a ring, redraw that spin from its conditional equilibrium distribution, keeping the others fixed. Writing σ−i\sigma_{-i}σ−i​ for all spins except spin iii, the rule is

hi(σ)=1n∑j≠iJijσj,P(σi←s∣σ−i)=eβshi(σ)2cosh⁡(βhi(σ)).\begin{aligned}h_i(\sigma)&=\frac{1}{\sqrt n}\sum_{j\ne i}J_{ij}\sigma_j,\\\mathbb P(\sigma_i\leftarrow s\mid\sigma_{-i})&=\frac{e^{\beta s h_i(\sigma)}}{2\cosh(\beta h_i(\sigma))}.\end{aligned}hi​(σ)P(σi​←s∣σ−i​)​=n​1​j=i∑​Jij​σj​,=2cosh(βhi​(σ))eβshi​(σ)​.​

Here s∈{−1,+1}s\in\{-1,+1\}s∈{−1,+1}, Jji=JijJ_{ji}=J_{ij}Jji​=Jij​, and 2cosh⁡u=eu+e−u2\cosh u=e^u+e^{-u}2coshu=eu+e−u. A redraw may leave the spin unchanged. The future depends only on the present configuration, making this a Markov chain. Its stationary distribution is πJ,β\pi_{J,\beta}πJ,β​.

One unit of time means approximately one attempted update per spin: nnn attempts altogether. Counting individual random-site attempts instead multiplies the relevant time scales by nnn. Confusing these clocks would change the critical exponent from 2/32/32/3 to 5/35/35/3.

Measuring the memory of an initial state

For distributions μ,ν\mu,\nuμ,ν on the configurations, their total-variation distance is

∥μ−ν∥TV=12∑σ∣μ(σ)−ν(σ)∣.\|\mu-\nu\|_{\mathrm{TV}}=\frac12\sum_\sigma|\mu(\sigma)-\nu(\sigma)|.∥μ−ν∥TV​=21​σ∑​∣μ(σ)−ν(σ)∣.

It is also the largest difference between their probabilities of the same event. Distance near zero means that no event reliably distinguishes the distributions.

Let Pt(x,⋅)P_t(x,\cdot)Pt​(x,⋅) be the law at time ttt starting from configuration xxx. Suppressing J,βJ,\betaJ,β in the notation, define

T(x)=inf⁡{t≥0:∥Pt(x,⋅)−π∥TV≤1/4},tmix=max⁡xT(x).\begin{aligned}T(x)&=\inf\{t\ge0:\|P_t(x,\cdot)-\pi\|_{\mathrm{TV}}\le1/4\},\\t_{\mathrm{mix}}&=\max_x T(x).\end{aligned}T(x)tmix​​=inf{t≥0:∥Pt​(x,⋅)−π∥TV​≤1/4},=xmax​T(x).​

The second quantity is the worst-start mixing time. A typical-start statement instead draws X0X_0X0​ from π\piπ, fixes that realized configuration, and studies T(X0)T(X_0)T(X0​). Averaging over the initial configuration before measuring distance gives equilibrium at every time, since ∑xπ(x)Pt(x,⋅)=π\sum_x\pi(x)P_t(x,\cdot)=\pi∑x​π(x)Pt​(x,⋅)=π. Forgetting a known initial configuration is a different question.

3. Development history and previous partial results

From equilibrium to dynamics

Sherrington and Kirkpatrick introduced their model in 1975 to study magnetism with competing random interactions. Their original paper concerns the equilibrium phases of an infinite-range model.

Parisi’s later description of equilibrium led to a formula for the limiting free energy, a quantity derived from log⁡Z\log ZlogZ. Guerra’s interpolation bound and Talagrand’s 2006 proof established that formula rigorously. This was a major equilibrium achievement, but a formula for the weights of configurations does not specify how quickly a local dynamics moves among them.

For critical dynamics, numerical work already pointed toward the scale n2/3n^{2/3}n2/3. Billoire and Campbell’s 2011 study, especially its finite-size scaling analysis, examined equilibrium spin autocorrelations. Such evidence suggests a relaxation scale; it does not establish a bound for every initial configuration.

Rigorous progress before this family

High-temperature results gradually extended the range of provably efficient local sampling. Eldan, Koehler, and Zeitouni obtained a spectral criterion giving an SK result for β<1/4\beta<1/4β<1/4. Later localization methods improved that range. In August 2026, Wang obtained optimal-order O(nlog⁡n)O(n\log n)O(nlogn) random-site mixing for every fixed β<1/2\beta<1/2β<1/2, including external fields. In September 2026, Boban, Li, and Oveis Gharan obtained polynomial mixing a fixed distance beyond 1/21/21/2. These advances still left a gap before the zero-field threshold 111.

The low-temperature story also depends on the starting state. Sellke’s 2025 preprint established exponential worst-case mixing at sufficiently low temperature. It explained why a physics prediction of stretched-exponential relaxation should not be interpreted as a worst-case bound. Rare, exceptionally slow configurations can dominate a maximum without describing an equilibrium sample.

Family 227 claims to close the high-temperature gap, identify the critical mixing exponent, and bound low-temperature relaxation for typical fixed equilibrium states. These are distinct advances with different quantifiers.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

The first six results below concern zero-field Gaussian disorder, with fixed β\betaβ as nnn grows. Probability tending to one refers to the random couplings and, for typical-start statements, the sampled initial state.

TemperatureClaimed scale in updates per spinStarting state
High temperature, 0≤β<10\le\beta<10≤β<1log⁡n\log nlogn, with cutoffWorst case
Critical, β=1\beta=1β=1n2/3+o(1)n^{2/3+o(1)}n2/3+o(1)Worst case
Low temperature, β>1\beta>1β>1Between two stretched exponentialsTypical fixed Gibbs state

High temperature and cutoff

The spectral-gap manuscript claims a positive relaxation rate independent of nnn for each fixed 0<β<10<\beta<10<β<1. A spectral gap measures how quickly the slowest mode of a reversible dynamics relaxes. This all-observables statement is stronger than controlling only linear combinations of spins.

The cutoff manuscript goes further. With dn(t)=max⁡x∥Pt(x,⋅)−π∥TVd_n(t)=\max_x\|P_t(x,\cdot)-\pi\|_{\mathrm{TV}}dn​(t)=maxx​∥Pt​(x,⋅)−π∥TV​, it claims a deterministic rate λ(β)>0\lambda(\beta)>0λ(β)>0 and location

tn=log⁡n2λ(β).t_n=\frac{\log n}{2\lambda(\beta)}.tn​=2λ(β)logn​.

For every fixed 0<ε<10<\varepsilon<10<ε<1, it claims dn((1−ε)tn)→1d_n((1-\varepsilon)t_n)\to1dn​((1−ε)tn​)→1 and dn((1+ε)tn)→0d_n((1+\varepsilon)t_n)\to0dn​((1+ε)tn​)→0, in probability over disorder. This abrupt drop on the relative time scale is called cutoff. The paper does not identify the smaller cutoff window or give a simple closed formula for λ(β)\lambda(\beta)λ(β).

The critical power law

The critical slowing-down manuscript claims that, at any deterministic time tn=o(n2/3)t_n=o(n^{2/3})tn​=o(n2/3), almost all Gibbs-sampled fixed states remain more than 1/41/41/4 from equilibrium. Here o(n2/3)o(n^{2/3})o(n2/3) means tn/n2/3→0t_n/n^{2/3}\to0tn​/n2/3→0.

The critical mixing manuscript supplies the claimed matching exponent for the worst start:

tmix=n2/3+o(1).t_{\mathrm{mix}}=n^{2/3+o(1)}.tmix​=n2/3+o(1).

Precisely, for every fixed δ>0\delta>0δ>0, the mixing time lies between n2/3−δn^{2/3-\delta}n2/3−δ and n2/3+δn^{2/3+\delta}n2/3+δ with probability tending to one. This does not give an exact constant or critical cutoff. In individual update attempts, the exponent is 5/35/35/3.

Low temperature and typical states

Combining the barrier manuscript with the typical-start upper bound gives, for every fixed β>1\beta>1β>1, the claimed bounds

exp⁡ ⁣(n1/10000)<T(X0)≤exp⁡ ⁣(n1−1/40000000)\exp\!\left(n^{1/10000}\right)<T(X_0)\le\exp\!\left(n^{1-1/40000000}\right)exp(n1/10000)<T(X0​)≤exp(n1−1/40000000)

with joint probability tending to one. Both bounds use rate-one clocks per spin and a fixed realized Gibbs start.

A stretched exponential exp⁡(na)\exp(n^a)exp(na), where 0<a<10<a<10<a<1, eventually exceeds every polynomial while growing more slowly than exp⁡(cn)\exp(cn)exp(cn) for fixed c>0c>0c>0. The enormous gap between the displayed exponents matters: these bounds classify the growth, but do not identify a sharp exponent such as the predicted 1/31/31/3. They also do not bound every starting state.

Universal critical memory curves

The two October manuscripts examine more than mixing time. At equilibrium, define the mean spin autocorrelation

Cn,J(t)=1n∑i=1nEπJ,1[σi(0)σi(t)].C_{n,J}(t)=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\mathbb E_{\pi_{J,1}}[\sigma_i(0)\sigma_i(t)].Cn,J​(t)=n1​i=1∑n​EπJ,1​​[σi​(0)σi​(t)].

The expectation averages the equilibrium initial state and the subsequent dynamics, keeping JJJ fixed. The stationary manuscript claims that n1/3Cn,J(sn2/3)n^{1/3}C_{n,J}(s n^{2/3})n1/3Cn,J​(sn2/3), for positive sss, converges in distribution as a function of time to a random limiting curve. Gaussian couplings and independent fair-sign couplings Jij=±1J_{ij}=\pm1Jij​=±1 give the same limiting law: this is universality. Individual disorder samples still have different curves.

The quench manuscript starts instead from independent fair spins, then runs the dynamics at β=1\beta=1β=1. A quench is this sudden change to the new temperature. The rescaled two-time correlation, with positive waiting time and lag both of order n2/3n^{2/3}n2/3, has a joint universal limit with the stationary curve. In that limit, increasing the waiting time recovers the stationary correlation. This is not a statement of universality for every coupling distribution.

5. Why the advance matters

If correct, the family turns the physical distinction between rapid equilibration, critical slowing, and persistent low-temperature memory into quantitative statements about a canonical random system. It also separates three questions that a single phrase such as “slow mixing” can hide: worst-case sampling, relaxation from typical equilibrium configurations, and the decay of particular observables.

For sampling algorithms, fast mixing gives a way to generate approximately equilibrium-distributed configurations by local updates. Low-temperature typical-start bounds, however, presuppose an equilibrium sample; they do not themselves provide an efficient method for obtaining one.

Importance: 4/5, provisional. The claimed transition across all fixed temperatures, the sharp critical exponent, and the universality results would constitute a major advance in probability and statistical mechanics. The score measures that mathematical significance if the claims hold. It is separate from verification, and will be calibrated against other families as the series grows.

6. The main idea

Independent spins explain the logarithm

At β=0\beta=0β=0, every redraw is a fair coin. Starting from all plus spins, the expected total magnetization at time ttt is ne−tne^{-t}ne−t: a spin retains its initial bias only if its clock has not rung. Equilibrium fluctuations of the total magnetization have scale n\sqrt nn​. Equating these scales gives

ne−t≈n⟹t≈12log⁡n.ne^{-t}\approx\sqrt n\quad\Longrightarrow\quad t\approx\tfrac12\log n.ne−t≈n​⟹t≈21​logn.

This calculation motivates the cutoff location but is not a full total-variation proof. With interactions, the cutoff manuscript tracks the sensitivity of evolved observables to individual spins. Upper bounds show that all distinguishability decays; lower bounds construct an observable whose initial bias remains detectable. The difficulty is making these estimates uniform over starting configurations.

Collective modes explain critical slowing

Think of diagonalizing a matrix to identify directions that respond weakly to a restoring force. Near criticality, certain collective spin directions become unusually soft. The manuscripts relate those directions to the largest eigenvalues of the normalized interaction matrix, with entries Jij/nJ_{ij}/\sqrt nJij​/n​, whose edge fluctuations occur on the scale n−2/3n^{-2/3}n−2/3.

This suggests a reciprocal time scale n2/3n^{2/3}n2/3, but Ising spins cannot simply be replaced by independent linear modes. The critical proofs compare them with auxiliary spherical spins—real vectors constrained to a sphere—and use progressively revealed noisy observations to control remaining fluctuations. They then transfer functional inequalities back to the discrete dynamics. The stationary and quench papers additionally identify the effective limiting evolution and compare Gaussian with sign disorder. These are proof strategies, not deductions from the eigenvalue scale alone.

Overlap detects barriers

The overlap between configurations is

R(σ,τ)=1n∑iσiτi.R(\sigma,\tau)=\frac1n\sum_i\sigma_i\tau_i.R(σ,τ)=n1​i∑​σi​τi​.

It equals one for identical configurations and minus one for opposite configurations. A single spin update changes it by at most 2/n2/n2/n, so local dynamics cannot jump across a macroscopic interval of overlaps.

The lower-bound paper uses constrained equilibrium comparisons and sequences of overlap crossings to obstruct rapid loss of memory for typical states. For the upper bound, the companion paper constructs probabilistic connections between sets of appreciable equilibrium mass, rules out excessively small flow between them, and converts that flow into typical-start mixing. Rare slow states can remain outside this conclusion. The two arguments explain why the lower and upper bounds concern a large fraction of states rather than a maximum over all states.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The pinned release’s family-specific Lean scope document describes partial coverage:

ClaimCoverage stated by the repository
High-temperature spectral gapDimension-independent bound for fixed 0<β<10<\beta<10<β<1
CutoffDiscrete-time ratio cutoff for 0≤β<1/20\le\beta<1/20≤β<1/2; the full range, explicit location, and continuous-time conclusion are outside this statement
Critical mixingWorst-start lower bound n2/3−εn^{2/3-\varepsilon}n2/3−ε and upper bound eεne^{\varepsilon n}eεn, for fixed ε>0\varepsilon>0ε>0; this does not certify the sharp upper exponent
Critical typical starts and linear observablesThe stated pre-n2/3n^{2/3}n2/3 obstruction and covariance/linear-relaxation bounds
Low-temperature barriersThe stated exp⁡(n1/10000)\exp(n^{1/10000})exp(n1/10000) obstruction for typical fixed starts

That document does not list formalizations of the sharp critical upper bound, the low-temperature typical-start upper bound, or the two universality manuscripts. This digest reports the published scope; no Lean build or independent audit of the complete proofs was performed for it.

The temperature is fixed before the system size tends to infinity. These statements do not automatically extend to nonzero fields, temperatures approaching criticality with nnn, all disorder laws, or finite-size numerical predictions. Universality here concerns the specified autocorrelation processes, not every mixing statement in the family. The repository README also explicitly allows for corrections to unformalized results.

8. Sources and further reading

The eight manuscripts

All eight papers are credited to OpenAI. Links below are pinned to the source revision used for this article; the numbered theorem locators are useful entry points.

  1. A spectral gap throughout the high-temperature Sherrington–Kirkpatrick phase — September 24, 2026; Theorem 1.1.
  2. Cutoff throughout the high-temperature Sherrington–Kirkpatrick phase — September 24, 2026; Theorem 1.1.
  3. Critical slowing down in the Sherrington–Kirkpatrick model — September 24, 2026; Theorems 1.2–1.3.
  4. Stretched-exponential barriers for typical SK initial states — September 24, 2026; Theorem 1.1.
  5. A typical-start upper bound for low-temperature SK Glauber dynamics — September 24, 2026; Theorem 1 and Corollary 2.
  6. Critical mixing in the Sherrington–Kirkpatrick model — September 25, 2026; Theorems 1.1–1.2.
  7. Functional universality of critical SK autocorrelations — October 5, 2026; Theorem 1.1.
  8. Universality of critical quench autocorrelations in the Sherrington–Kirkpatrick model — October 5, 2026; Theorem 1.1.

Historical sources are linked in Section 3. Optional background: Wikipedia’s Markov chain, Gibbs measure, and total-variation distance entries. Essential definitions are given above.
